item.title: Introducing object enrichments: Transform unstructured data into agent-ready context
item.description:
The vast majority of enterprise information is unstructured, locked away in object storage as petabytes of images, PDFs, videos, and audio files. This data holds the institutional knowledge AI agents need to do business-critical work. But to an agent, a raw object is just bytes it can't reason over. As enterprises start to deploy agents in production, the focus has shifted toward transforming these raw objects into rich, agent-ready context.

Today, we are introducing object enrichments, a new Google Cloud Storage capability that uses AI models to automatically extract rich contextual metadata from Cloud Storage objects and saves it in-place as object context, enabling agents to acquire the information needed to make complex business decisions. Object enrichments gives customers access to the AI models used by internal Google services such as Google Photos, offering image annotations like object detection and image labeling at 75% cost savings when compared to similar services from other cloud providers. Available in preview, this fully managed service also includes high-quality PDF classification model, enabling customers to seamlessly turn their object store into an intelligent, AI-ready foundation.

“L'Oreal is the 4th largest advertiser in the world, and managing media assets at that scale is complex. Cloud Storage object enrichments’s high quality and cost-effective annotations enable us to discover, understand, and govern our content at scale, accelerating marketing and advertising operations while remaining compliant in all markets. Object enrichments enables L'Oreal to label its extensive creative asset repository 100x faster at a fraction of the cost of existing pipelines and processes.” – Antoine Castex, Principal Data & AI Architect, L’Oreal

Agents need context, not raw bytes

To operate efficiently, agents need grounded knowledge; however, reading every raw file at scale is cost- and performance-prohibitive. For example, if an operations agent needs to pinpoint a specific event—such as a doorstep package delivery or a roadway hazard—streaming thousands of smart-camera or vehicle frames into the AI model on every user prompt would burn through expensive tokens and add minutes of delay. To bridge this gap, teams must pre-process raw data and extract rich, contextual metadata, which agents can then leverage at runtime. Historically, achieving this meant dealing with three challenges:

  • Cost: Running models over millions to billions of objects is expensive, pushing organizations to compromise and process only a fraction of their data, creating blind spots that lessen agents’ accuracy.

  • Operational toil: A self-managed pipeline means stitching together multiple services — from event triggers and queues to custom infrastructure built on Cloud Run or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) — along with scalable retry/error logic and job scheduling. Once deployed, that infrastructure still requires continuous upgrades and capacity management. Teams sometimes spend months on this plumbing rather than focusing on building agents that solve actual business problems. 

  • Fragmented metadata: Extracted metadata often lands in a separate data store, decoupling context from the bytes it describes. Teams must pay for and maintain a second storage system, govern access policies across disconnected permission models, and run custom cleanup jobs to keep metadata in sync when source objects are copied, moved, or deleted.

This is why we built object enrichments: to natively provide agent-ready context for your unstructured data, equipping your agents with complete, grounded knowledge without prohibitive costs, custom pipeline plumbing, or fragmented metadata.

Key benefits of object enrichments

1. Reduce costs with Google models
Object enrichments offers dramatic savings at scale: enriching 10 million images or PDFs costs just $700 (according to published pricing). You can use Google’s high-quality AI models for image annotations—including object detection, face detection, image labeling, and explicit content detection—at one of the industry’s best price points. In addition, the PDF classification model lets you categorize documents into standard business and industry categories like Finance, Games, News, and Health.

"Even with a highly accurate baseline, Hyperscience leveraged object enrichments to drive a 50%+ lift in document classification accuracy, while simultaneously reducing classification inference costs by 2-3x.” – Mayur Pillay, VP Partnerships, Hyperscience

2. Generate richer context with Gemini
For complex multimodal reasoning across text, PDFs, images, audio, and video, you can leverage Gemini natively with object enrichments, unlocking advanced use cases such as summarization, entity extraction, transcription, and translation. Please reach out to us at redacted@example.invalid to learn more and request access to this upcoming functionality.

3. No pipeline, low toil setup
Skip the brittle, multi-component DIY pipelines. Setting up an enrichment job just takes three simple steps, with no code required in the Google Cloud console, or programmatically via the Cloud Storage API, following these steps:

  1. Define your scope: Provide a set of buckets containing the objects to process and specify the processing location. Object enrichments can scale to millions or billions of objects.

  2. Choose your models: Pick one or more of the five first-party Cloud Storage models for images and PDFs.

  3. Grant permissions: Grant the necessary IAM permissions to the object enrichments service to access your Cloud Storage buckets.

Object enrichments handles the rest: It orchestrates model inference, parses the responses, and writes the results to each object's object context, with built-in retries and throttling. There are no queues to manage, workers to scale, or glue code to maintain.

"Cloud Storage object enrichments and BigQuery, slashes AI development from 6 months to 1 month while rapidly improving our models." - Brandon Bunker, VP of Product AI, Vivint

4. Context lives where the bytes live
Instead of parking metadata in a separate data store, object enrichments writes model outputs directly to object context, a specialized Cloud Storage metadata construct that’s purpose-built for storing contextual information as structured key-value pairs alongside the object itself. Because context is stored alongside object’s actual bytes, you get enterprise-grade data management out of the box, with:

  • Cloud Storage durability and simplified lifecycle management: Object context shares the same durability and consistency properties as the underlying Cloud Storage object. It travels automatically with the object during copy, move, and replication operations and is automatically removed when the object is deleted — no more cleanup jobs!

  • Fine-grained IAM governance: Using IAM, administrators can control who can read, add, update, or remove object context.

  • Fast object filtering and serving: Applications can filter object listings directly by object context key-value pairs or read context metadata alongside objects, in order to serve richer experiences.

  • Turnkey multimodal analytics in BigQuery: You can easily configure your object context to natively flow into BigQuery via Storage Insights datasets, allowing data teams to run SQL analytics, build dashboards, and join unstructured file insights with structured enterprise tables, without writing a single line of ETL code.

What customers are building

Early customers are already putting object enrichments to work across key business scenarios:

  • Creative asset search and media archives: Marketing, retail, and media organizations manage petabytes of creative image assets, where finding a specific asset, e.g., "a red car driving at sunset" or "a vintage convertible in the desert during golden hour", requires rich semantic metadata. Object enrichments automatically generates descriptive labels in object context, which can then be indexed into a vector database or BigQuery to power accurate retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications and asset-discovery agents.

  • Automated trust, safety, and content moderation: Social platforms, marketplaces, and digital media pipelines scan millions of user uploads and supplier catalogs every day for explicit content. Historically, scaling this for every single upload has been cost-prohibitive, but not anymore. With object enrichments, you can process 10 million images for just $700.

  • Training data curation for frontier AI: Autonomous driving, smart home, and robotics companies capture hundreds of millions of raw camera and sensor files. They often need targeted data samples for specific fine-tuning scenarios, which make up only a tiny fraction of their corpus. By enriching raw captures in place with object detection and image labeling models and then querying the resulting metadata in BigQuery, ML engineers can pinpoint exact training cohorts in minutes rather than months.

  • Multimodal analytics: Combine insights from images and documents with structured business data to drive personalization, fraud detection, and trend discovery — for example, analyzing customer uploaded images of the product alongside their comments and recent sales data.

Get started with object enrichments

Object enrichments is available in preview today in the Cloud Storage console and through the Cloud Storage API. To get started, check out the following resources

  • Read the documentation: Learn how to configure an enrichments job and use object contexts.

  • Analyze in BigQuery: Set up Storage Insights datasets and query your enrichments alongside your BigQuery business data.

  • Connect your agents: Pair object enrichments and object context with the Cloud Storage MCP server to give agents secure, IAM-scoped access to your data and its context.

  • Review pricing: See Cloud Storage pricing for details.

  • Gemini enrichments: Reach out to us at redacted@example.invalid to learn more and request access to this upcoming functionality.

  • Start building: Head to the Cloud Storage console to enrich your first bucket in just three clicks.

item.title: Building an agentic stack in Envoy: routing models, tokens, and MCP
item.description:
At Google Cloud, we believe the next generation of AI and agentic systems must be built on open, battle-tested foundations. Envoy, an open-source edge and service proxy designed for cloud-native applications, has already transformed microservices and modern cloud networking, powering everything from Google Cloud’s Application Load Balancers to the Agent Substrate dataplane on Google Kubernetes Engine. Now, Envoy is uniquely positioned to become the open standard for AI traffic, MCP tooling, and agent-to-agent communication. 

Earlier this year, we presented the technical case for Envoy networking in the agentic AI era, examining how autonomous AI agents fundamentally challenge traditional Layer 7 networking assumptions. Unlike microservices, autonomous agent workloads choose who they communicate with. In addition, their routing attributes live deep within request bodies, with their traffic governed by token budgets as well as request rates, and their multi-turn reasoning loops requiring stateful session affinity and strict tool execution boundaries.

At Google Cloud, we have been working hard to develop Envoy for the agentic era. Read on for a closer look at how Envoy has evolved to better support autonomous agents, giving developers the performance and portability of an open-source ecosystem, backed by enterprise security and scalability.

Why autonomous agents challenge traditional L7 proxies

Over the past decade, Envoy became the industry standard for cloud-native traffic management by operating cleanly at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP connection management) and Layer 7 (URI, method, and header-based routing).

Autonomous agents introduce two higher-order protocol layers:

  • Layer 8 (agentic interaction protocols): such as LLM APIs, Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Google’s Agent2Agent (A2A), running over JSON-RPC 2.0 or gRPC. Critical policy attributes—such as tools/call, tool_name: "execute_sql", or model: "gemini-1.5-pro"—are serialized inside the request payload.

  • Layer 9 (agent framework interfaces): Coordination frameworks such as UCP, AP2, and Google Cloud’s Agent Development Kit, where multi-turn workflows produce dynamic token consumption and non-linear execution graphs.

Fronting these workloads with traditional L7 proxies creates four major architectural challenges:

  1. Payload blindness: Nearly all LLM traffic shares the same paths (such as /v1/chat/completions), so a header-based proxy cannot distinguish between a low-cost query and an expensive 500,000-token prompt, or one model from another.

  2. Request rate limiting fallacy: One request  per minute with a massive context window can use  more accelerator compute and memory bandwidth than dozens of  short queries, and agent loops can burn through budgets unnoticed.

  3. Stateless load balancing: Each turn of an agent's conversation should go back to the server that already remembers it. Traditional load balancers send it to whichever server is next, so the model has to start over for every turn, this wastes time and GPUs.

  4. Ungoverned tool execution: Agents query databases, execute code in sandboxes, and call third-party APIs. Without inline inspection of MCP tool  calls, organizations risk prompt injection, data exfiltration, and runaway billing loops.

The core pillars of Envoy’s agentic stack

To address these challenges, Envoy provides capabilities that turn the network into an active governance layer:

Core Pillar

Operational Functionality

1. Native body parser

Payload blindness: Read request bodies, not just headers.Line-rate payload normalization across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini schemas with SSE stream handling.

2. Tokenomics engine

Request-rate fallacy: Count tokens, not just requests.Pre-inference token estimation, tokens per minute (TPM)/tokens per day (TPD) rate limiting

3. Model & MCP routing

Stateless load balancing: Keep agent sessions on the right serversEndpoint Picker (EPP) model dispatch, KV-cache prefix affinity, MCP Stateless support.

4. AI security guardrails

Ungoverned tool execution: Policy tool calls.Inline policy, decision point (ext_proc) callouts for guardrails: Model Armor, ShieldGemma, and data loss prevention.

1. Native wire-format body parsing and transcoding

Client applications often get locked into specific model APIs. For example, client code built for OpenAI's schema cannot communicate with Anthropic's endpoints or Google’s Gemini without client-side translation layers.

To help, Envoy ecosystem includes native body parsers that normalize requests across diverse model families, providing:

  • Client abstraction: Upstream applications send a standardized schema. Envoy inspects the JSON payload at line-rate, extracts the target model, and dynamically transcodes the request into the downstream provider's native format.

  • No application code changes: Switching from an external commercial model to a self-hosted open-source model (such as Gemma or Llama on vLLM) requires only an Envoy configuration update. Application code remains unchanged.

  • Streaming token extraction: Envoy parses server-sent events (SSE) response streams in real time, capturing token counts from usage chunks while maintaining ultra-low time-to-first-token latency.

2. Tokenomics engine: token-aware traffic management

In AI networking, tokens are the fundamental unit of capacity. Envoy replaces coarse request counters with token-aware traffic management features such as:

  • Token rate limiting: Enforces tokens per minute (TPM) and tokens per day (TPD) limits per tenant, project, or model.

  • Pre-inference throttling: Envoy estimates input tokens from request payload bytes and extracts actual token usage from LLM responses to record in a quota database, rejecting subsequent over-quota requests with an HTTP 429 before they reach the inference cluster.

  • Runaway loop protection: Autonomous agents can enter recursive reasoning loops. By tracking cumulative token consumption and message counts per session or agent ID, Envoy throttles multi-turn sessions once an agent exceeds its assigned budget.

3. Model routing and Model Context Protocol (MCP) support

Envoy manages traffic for both downstream model backends and outbound tool calls, with:

  • KV-cache prefix affinity: Using the Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extensions and Endpoint Picker (EPP), Envoy routes prompts sharing identical system instructions to the GPU worker currently holding that cache in memory, reducing latency.

  • Model retry and fallback: If a primary model returns a 429 status code or fails, Envoy automatically retries or redirects the request to a secondary model pool with zero client interruption.

  • MCP tool routing: For MCP agents, Envoy routes requests via JSON-RPC 2.0 bodies and HTTP headers. Per the 2026-07-28 MCP specification, Envoy uses Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers for zero-body-parsing routing to backend servers. Backends reject header-body mismatches with an HTTP 400 / -32020 (HeaderMismatch) error to prevent tampering.

4. AI security guardrails 

Inline safety filtering cannot come at the expense of network throughput. To prevent this, Envoy provides security callouts: Using standardized external processing (ext_proc), Envoy connects to dedicated policy decision engines — such as Google Cloud’s Model Armor, ShieldGemma, or local classifiers — to detect prompt injections and sensitive data leaks with minimal latency overhead.

High-density infrastructure: Envoy and Agent Substrate

In enterprise production environments, agents frequently spend time idle between user queries or long-running tool executions. Running hundreds of thousands of idle agents in dedicated containers or virtual machines can create prohibitive infrastructure costs.

Envoy pairs directly with high-density execution runtimes like Agent Substrate to provide:

  • Scale-to-zero traffic steering: Agent Substrate uses lightweight isolation runtimes (such as Cloud Hypervisor, microVMs and gVisor application sandboxes) that can suspend and resume in milliseconds. When traffic arrives for a suspended agent, Envoy buffers the initial packet while signaling the runtime to resume the instance, completing the end-to-end resume in milliseconds.

  • Egress perimeter defense: Envoy functions as both an ingress and egress gateway for agent environments, routing the inbound traffic and restricting outbound network calls to verified domains and preventing untrusted autonomous code from reaching unauthorized endpoints.

Getting started

Envoy has evolved into an intelligent, extensible networking layer designed specifically for the unique demands of multi-agent architectures. To begin building with the agentic stack in Envoy:

  • Explore the code: Review the Envoy proxy and Agent Router implementations on Github and examine the open-source sample configurations.

  • Join the community: Participate in CNCF, Gateway API, and Kubernetes AI Gateway Working Group to collaborate on standardized inference APIs, MCP routing specifications, and token management conventions.

item.title: Beyond the compute bottleneck: Maximizing the ROI of AI accelerators with purpose-built storage
item.description:
There’s a lot more to AI infrastructure than just buying accelerators. Indeed, the infrastructure mandate for enterprise AI has shifted from acquiring accelerators to keeping them fully utilized. Next to these expensive accelerators, storage accounts for only a small sliver of total AI spend. However, having the wrong storage in place can put the rest of your committed compute capital at risk.

To optimize your accelerators’ TCO, you need to keep them fully occupied. Very often, the challenge here is data I/O. If accelerators sit waiting to read or write data, you’re wasting money. Across the industry, insufficient storage throughput has become a primary impediment to AI success, starving models of the data they need. And the problem is only going to get worse. Gartner predicts enterprises will deploy over 150,000 agents in the next few years, so the I/O bottleneck and the challenge of orchestrating storage for agentic fleets will only compound. 

Organizations are eager to move their AI initiatives forward, but preventing idle compute requires a purpose-built approach to data I/O. With the demands of AI, standard enterprise storage — even a system optimized for fast analytics — will inevitably suffer from bottlenecks that leave compute resources twiddling their proverbial thumbs.

AI is not a monolithic workload

The most common architectural misstep we see is treating AI as a single, general-purpose workload. In reality, the physical movement of data transforms across the AI lifecycle, creating distinct I/O profiles based on how models consume and generate information:

  • In model training, clusters read datasets at high throughput, but pause regularly to write checkpoints to record their state in event of a failure. When thousands of GPUs attempt to save this data in a single, simultaneous burst, standard storage architectures stall. That’s especially true of traditional cloud storage, which is engineered for durability. Writing checkpoints triggers thousands of administrative database transactions to safely record the files, bogging down the system, choking the network, and freezing the entire GPU cluster until the save is complete. Furthermore, saving the data is only one of the problems: If a server fails, slow storage turns a routine checkpoint recovery into a multi-hour delay, leaving expensive accelerators sitting completely idle.

  • Inference, conversely, is real-time and latency-sensitive. As AI services scale to meet user demand, inference clusters constantly load and unload petabyte-scale model repositories quickly. In this case, a slow storage system can leave GPUs in a “cold start” as they wait for data.  Also, many models now process context windows that exceed 100,000 tokens, filling up accelerator memory. Without a high-speed external cache to offload this context, when a user asks the next question, the accelerator must recalculate previous inputs, wasting compute on redundant operations.

Industry-leading performance across object and file storage

To solve these I/O challenges and keep expensive accelerators busy, organizations need compute, networking, and storage to be deeply integrated.

As industry analysts have noted, enterprise customers gain a unique performance advantage because Google Cloud runs on the exact same storage foundation as Google's own consumer products. This foundation is built on Colossus—the planet-scale distributed file system powering Google Search, YouTube, and Gemini. Because this shared infrastructure supports billions of users daily, its reliability is continuously proven against the extreme traffic and hardware demands of Google's global consumer services. As a result, today, nine out of the world’s ten leading AI frontier model labs run on Google Cloud infrastructure because we deliver the throughput and performance they require to innovate. In fact, we spent the last two years co-designing our storage architecture directly with these frontier labs as well as with Google's own foundation model teams.

 For large-scale training on object storage, our architecture ensures workloads don’t have to wait on data, and successfully absorbs peak bandwidth demands.  For real-time inference, enterprise platform companies like Salesforce AI Research leverage our architecture to serve complex agentic inference workloads with up to 40% fewer GPUs. We deliver these outcomes through two distinct, purpose-built storage solutions:

  • Cloud Storage Rapid: For organizations that have standardized on cloud-native object storage, Cloud Storage Rapid provides Colossus scale and performance directly to accelerators, so they can use the data stored on object storage in their AI workflows. This eliminates the need to migrate data into separate, specialized storage silos to achieve the performance that AI workloads require. A single Rapid bucket pushes the boundaries of object storage, delivering up to 15 TB/s of throughput and 20 million queries per second with sub-millisecond latency. This makes it a strong fit for streaming large training datasets and recovering checkpoints without bottlenecking the network.

    For bursty workloads such as model loading across multiple locations, Rapid Cache acts as a read accelerator that co-locates active data directly with TPU and GPU clusters. With no code changes, Rapid Cache delivers up to 2.5 TB/s of aggregate read throughput, taking idle cold-start times from hours to minutes.

  • Google Cloud Managed Lustre: For demanding AI and HPC workloads that need a parallel file system, there’s Google Cloud Managed Lustre. Built in partnership with DDN, Managed Lustre provides up to 10 TB/s of throughput per instance, absorbing the intense read-write bursts of synchronous checkpointing and reinforcement learning, so that your expensive accelerators remain fully saturated.

    To help organizations scale their workloads without breaking budgets, Managed Lustre’s new Dynamic Tier delivers more Lustre for less by consolidating hot and cold data into a single namespace, eliminating traditional caching performance cliffs. Finally, Managed Lustre Cloud Storage Mirror reduces the downtime and operational friction inherent in manual data transfers. Instead of you having to write custom scripts that leave expensive compute clusters waiting on files, it automatically synchronizes datasets in the background so they are ready before training begins.

Proven in production at scale

This purpose-built storage foundation is already powering customers’ most demanding AI workloads, helping them extract maximum return on investment from their compute resources.

  • Thinking Machines Lab utilizes Cloud Storage Rapid Cache to stabilize read throughput peaks above 1.8 TB/s and achieve an 89% cache hit ratio, completely eradicating rate-limiting surge errors across their multi-region architecture.

  • Shopify deployed 50+ unique Rapid Caches across their worldwide footprint, achieving over 2 TB/s peak throughput and up to a 90% latency reduction from their baseline to meet the data demands of their growing compute scale.

  • Salesforce AI Research uses Managed Lustre as a high-throughput, low-latency external cache to keep their GPUs fully saturated, driving substantial performance gains for LLM inference over previous hardware generations.

  • Atlassian adopted Managed Lustre on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to turn preemption interruptions into quick five-minute restores, delivering nearly 5x higher throughput and boosting their GPU utilization by 70% compared to NVMe-based systems.

  • Harmonic relies on Managed Lustre to train mathematical reasoning models, eliminating 50% of experiment interruptions, cutting startup times in half, and increasing data retrieval speeds by 15x.

The path forward

When advising AI Infrastructure teams designing their stack today, our guidance is straightforward. First, evaluate your token economics rather than just legacy storage metrics. If your chips are waiting on data, optimizing storage is a cost-effective and efficient remedy. Second, avoid creating separate copies of data for every new workload; keep your primary data in a unified foundation and move it to the right tier as needed. Finally, while AI performance grabs the headlines, you can’t create your AI strategy on infrastructure built for a different era. At the same time, AI infrastructure needs enterprise-grade reliability, built-in security, and automated cost discipline for optimized TCO.

The future of enterprise AI belongs to organizations that can turn their data into action. Google Cloud enables you to match the speed of your storage to the speed of your compute, so that you maximize your compute investments.

item.title: Introducing TPU Sync: Fast KV cache and weight transfer for inference and RL on TPU
item.description:
As frontier AI evolves from stateless single-turn prompts to million-token agents, disaggregated serving, and continuous reinforcement learning (RL), the primary bottleneck in AI infrastructure has shifted from raw compute to orchestrating live model state — both the contextual state held in massive key-value (KV) caches during inference and the parameter state updated and broadcast from trainers to rollout samplers during RL. Whenever this state is trapped inside a single chip's memory or stalled on network transfers, AI accelerators sit idle.

We designed TPU Sync from first principles to serve as the model-state layer across TPU clusters — built on the architectural insight that accelerator High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network (DCN) should operate as a single, co-designed memory hierarchy. An open-source, native C++ library, TPU Sync moves TPU-tiled tensors directly across this hierarchy with asynchronous DMA transfers that overlap data movement with active computation.

For inference, it decouples TPU compute from network backpressure and turns host DRAM, local SSDs, and Google Cloud Managed Lustre into an automated, multi-tier KV cache; and for RL, it exposes low-level DMA and DCN primitives that higher-level RL frameworks can use to stream updated weights from trainers to samplers. By accessing device buffers in place rather than copying or locking them, TPU Sync consistently slashes KV transfer latency by over 90% and reduces Time to First Token (TTFT) by an average of 90% for heavyweight open-weight MoE models (235B–480B parameters) in prefix-caching and disaggregated-serving workloads, compared to running without TPU Sync.

Across this shared model-state layer, TPU Sync integrates directly into existing infrastructure stacks across PyTorch (via TorchTPU) and JAX — serving as the TPU KV cache connector for vLLM, SGLang, and llm-d disaggregated serving, while providing low-level transfer primitives for Pathways and multi-controller JAX (McJAX) RL pipelines.

Understanding TPU Sync: The kitchen analogy

To understand TPU Sync’s impact, imagine a high-end restaurant kitchen. Think of the TPU as an incredibly fast executive chef working on a tiny countertop (the chip's HBM). When preparing a massive feast, the chef needs lots of ingredients (the KV cache), which quickly clutter the counter.

  • The standard kitchen (without TPU Sync): When the small counter fills up, the chef has to toss out prepped ingredients and chop them again from scratch the next time an order needs them — stalling the kitchen on repetitive prep work (prefill recomputation).

  • The upgraded kitchen (with TPU Sync): TPU Sync adds a spacious side pantry (pinned host RAM), a shared walk-in cold storage room accessible to every station in the kitchen (shared cluster storage), and a coordinated team of runners. The runners slide full prep trays directly between the counter, the pantry, and peer stations without repacking them (direct DMA in native TPU layout).

Crucially, the runners swap trays in and out while the chef keeps cooking (asynchronous, non-blocking transfers).

Key use cases for TPU Sync

TPU Sync improves system throughput and latency in workloads requiring deep context, high concurrency, multi-turn reasoning and RL rollouts:

  • Long-context AI agents and multi-turn chats: When interacting with an AI agent over an extended 256K to 1M+ token session or analyzing massive documents, the model generates a continuously growing KV cache. Instead of allowing this state to exhaust HBM capacity, TPU Sync automatically tiers older KV blocks out of TPU HBM and into large pools of host RAM (with experimental tiering to shared secondary storage).

  • Enterprise applications with heavy system prompts (prefix caching): AI serving platforms receive thousands of queries that share common instructions or documents. Rather than recomputing prefixes that the model has already processed, TPU Sync extends the prefix cache into distributed host memory so concurrent sessions can reuse precomputed KV blocks and bypass redundant prefill computation.

  • Disaggregated serving architecture (prefill/decode): In modern enterprise deployments, workloads are isolated: Compute-bound nodes process the initial massive prompt (prefill), while memory-bound nodes draft the response token-by-token (decode). TPU Sync bridges this hardware gap by acting as a high-bandwidth Host-to-Host (H2H) streaming pipeline. It routes the processed context directly from the prefill nodes to the decode nodes, consistently delivering an over 90% reduction in data transfer overhead.

  • Reinforcement learning pipelines (experimental): Validated on internal RL workloads and included in the repository as an experimental module, TPU Sync provides low-level DMA and DCN transfer primitives that higher-level RL frameworks can use to synchronize model weights between trainers and inference samplers — including automatic resharding across different trainer and sampler parallelism layouts — to reduce the time rollout workers spend waiting on weight updates.

Breaking through the memory wall with TPU Sync

At its core, TPU Sync establishes a high-performance data transfer path between TPU HBM and host RAM, as well as across TPU hosts via the DCN. It achieves this through four key architectural advantages:

  • Layout-preserving direct DMA with in-place buffer aliasing: TPU Sync accesses the underlying JAX PJRT buffers or PyTorch tensors in place and moves slices directly between TPU HBM and page-locked (DmaMap-registered) host memory in a single hardware DMA. By keeping tensors in their native TPU physical tile layout across HBM, host DRAM, storage, and the wire, data lands ready for immediate Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU) execution with no Python serialization, no layout conversion, and no user-space bounce buffers.

  • Compute-overlapped transfers: Rather than taking an exclusive lock or making an on-device copy of static KV cache and weight buffers, TPU Sync creates raw PJRT buffer aliases (PJRT_RawBuffer) without holding PJRT usage locks so block-level transfers can run concurrently with active in-place computation, with built-in DMA pacing to keep large transfers from delaying kernel launches.

  • No XLA compilation in the data path: Because TPU Sync executes transfers and tile-aware strided resharding in native C++ outside the XLA graph, moving KV blocks or resharding weights across different trainer and sampler topologies does not trigger runtime compilation — keeping the data path fast and framework-agnostic.

  • High-bandwidth PCIe DMA and DCN streaming: Using the raw_transfer library’s direct PJRT raw-buffer DMA pipeline, TPU Sync reaches up to 223 GB/s of aggregate D2H and H2D throughput per Ironwood (TPU v7x) host out of the 256 GB/s PCIe Gen5 hardware ceiling, and streams across the DCN at up to ~192 Gbps on a single 200 Gbps NIC (or ~350 Gbps across dual 200 Gbps NICs with NUMA-aware multi-NIC striping).

TPU Sync exposes a low-level data transfer API, making it easier for developers to integrate high-speed TPU data transfer into higher-level frameworks.

Higher-level architecture

Built on top of its core transport and resharding primitives, TPU Sync provides a modular orchestration stack for distributed cache management:

  • Global KV store: A global registry that maps prompt prefix hashes to physical cache blocks, handles dynamic lookups, and coordinates LRU eviction and tier demotion.

  • TPU Sync controller: The orchestration layer that generates transfer plans, coordinates data movement across nodes, and handles lease management and recovery.

  • KV cache manager: The local execution engine that tracks block states, manages HBM, host DRAM (including /dev/shm warm-boot persistence) alongside experimental POSIX storage backends, and executes asynchronous DMA transfers.

Solving disaggregated serving and prefix caching

Let us take a closer look at how TPU Sync helps with some of the use cases we listed in the earlier section. By treating host pinned memory as a substantial, high-speed Tier 2 cache, TPU Sync reduces the fragmentation and memory limits of standard HBM setups.

Prefill/Decode (P/D) disaggregated serving

In state-of-the-art serving topologies, prefill (compute-bound) and decode (memory-bound) phases are isolated on separate node pools. To prevent latency bubbles, TPU Sync bridges this gap with a highly optimized, three-step pipeline:

  1. Direct-DMA offloading: Once a prefill node processes an initial prompt, TPU Sync immediately moves the resulting KV blocks into pinned host RAM via its asynchronous D2H DMA path.

  2. Host-to-host streaming: The TPU Sync controller then orchestrates a high-bandwidth Host-to-Host (H2H) transfer, streaming the context directly to the assigned decode node.

  3. Overlapped ingestion: As blocks arrive in the decode node's host RAM, TPU Sync triggers an asynchronous H2D transfer directly into TPU HBM. This happens concurrently with active decoding computation, substantially minimizing TTFT.

Host-powered prefix caching

For highly concurrent systems sharing large system prompts or running multi-turn agentic loops, TPU HBM is not large enough to hold multiple active cache blocks. TPU Sync extends the prefix cache out of HBM (Tier 1) into substantial, distributed host RAM pools (Tier 2). Because TPU Sync transfers are asynchronous, it overlaps the PCIe DMA loading of the next required prefix from host RAM with the compute of the current request — minimizing TPU idle time between requests.

For workloads that exceed even host DRAM capacity, TPU Sync also includes an experimental POSIX storage backend (Tier 3+) that asynchronously spills older KV blocks to local SSDs or shared Google Cloud Managed Lustre storage — pairing with llm-d prefix-affinity routing on GKE so replicas can recall cached prefixes across tiers without recomputing prompts.

Sample performance results

P/D disaggregated inference result highlights: 

  • Over 90% KV transfer overhead cut: For heavyweight models like Qwen3 235B, median KV transfer latency dropped from several seconds down to a flat ~230 ms.

  • Substantial TTFT reduction: Demonstrated an average of 60% reduction in TTFT for heavyweight models (Qwen3 235B) under controlled, low-concurrency testing benchmarks, and an average of 90% for 480B under low concurrency.

  • Substantial high-traffic scalability: During sustained traffic spikes, TPU Sync achieves an average of 30% to 70% increase in token output throughput for 235B, depending on traffic distribution.

Prefix caching result highlights: 

  • Expands KV cache capacity beyond HBM: When heavyweight MoE model weights consume most of device HBM, on-chip memory can hold only a few long-context prefixes. Offloading into pinned host DRAM expands effective cache capacity by an order of magnitude.

  • Sustains high cache-hit rates under concurrency: Pooling distributed host RAM keeps shared system prompts and multi-turn agent contexts warm across thousands of concurrent sessions instead of thrashing HBM.

  • Significantly reduces prefill recompute: Directly bypasses heavy compute layers for repeated instruction blocks and system prompts, reducing average TTFT by up to 90% on 64K-context workloads while delivering over 50% higher throughput and a 30% reduction in P99 inter-token latency (ITL).

Please see the note1 below on the testing configuration. 

Ecosystem adoption and partnerships

TPU Sync serves as the open, composable memory substrate across our PyTorch-on-TPU and Kubernetes serving ecosystem, built in close collaboration with key open-source maintainers and infrastructure partners:

  • Inferact (vLLM-TorchTPU): Co-engineered with Inferact, maintainers of vLLM-TorchTPU, TPU Sync is integrated directly via vLLM's native KVConnector interface. It powers Direct-DMA host DRAM offloading and multi-host P/D disaggregation across frontier open-source models.

  • RadixArk (SGLang-TorchTPU): In partnership with RadixArk, maintainers of SGLang-TorchTPU, TPU Sync serves as both the high-speed P/D disaggregation transfer backend and the native I/O backend for SGLang’s hierarchical cache.

  • llm-d 1.0 integration: llm-d 1.0 pairs with TPU Sync on GKE to deliver global prefix-cache-affinity routing, per-rank decode session pinning, and experimental two-stage capacity spill to Google Cloud Managed Lustre.

  • Validated by frontier AI labs and enterprises: Frontier AI organizations are already adopting our PyTorch-on-TPU serving stack and evaluating TPU Sync multi-tier architectures for production deployments — including Meta, alongside major enterprises like Wayfair, and multi-silicon partners.

Get started 

TPU Sync is available today as open source with Python wheels for both PyTorch (tpu-sync-torch) and JAX (tpu-sync-jax), and is integrated with vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU, and llm-d on GKE. Visit the GitHub repository to explore the architecture docs, C++ and Python APIs, and deployment guides.

We are committed to working with the open-source community to advance the model-state layer on TPU — supporting new frontier architectures, expanded storage tiering, and longer-horizon agentic and RL workloads. For more up-to-date performance results, please see our ongoing efforts on public benchmarks (InferenceX).

1. Performance results are based on internal testing conducted in July 2026 on TPU v7x (2x2x1 topology), configured with PCIe Gen5 (x16) per TPU chip and one or two 200 Gbps NICs enabled per host, running tpu-inference v0.24.0 (using JAX 0.10.2 and libtpu 0.0.42.1). Metrics presented represent average and median performance improvements observed under controlled laboratory conditions. Actual real-world performance, cache hit rates, and latency reductions will vary based on system configuration, network bandwidth, concurrent traffic, and specific user workload patterns.

item.title: Our newest TPUs: 8tx and 8i Max, built for the agentic era
item.description:
Editor’s note: This blog was originally published on News from Google.

We first designed TPUs more than a decade ago motivated by Google’s internal demands, including voice recognition and language translation. Eight generations of TPUs later, the use cases have exploded, covering: i) training and serving our own Gemini models, ii) agentic workloads, iii) delivering services to Google Cloud customers on our cloud infrastructure, and most recently, iv) allowing customers to deploy TPUs directly into their own data centers. TPUs are now a rapidly growing business with nearly 100 customers — including frontier labs, trading firms, retailers, universities, and more.

At Google Cloud Next in April, we introduced two new specialized TPUs in the same generation — 8t for large-scale training and 8i for real-time reasoning. TPU 8t and 8i offer up to 2.7 times better training performance and 80% better inference price performance, respectively, versus our previous generation of TPUs. 

Today, we’re taking that a step further, expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with two additional systems: TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack, and TPU 8tx for secure and confidential inference. This is the first time we have introduced four TPU systems in a single year.

While we’ve always co-designed our TPUs in partnership with Google DeepMind, we’re now increasingly getting feedback from external organizations on their specific needs. With computing moving from human to agent scale, businesses are asking for accelerators that can reason across AI models’ massive context windows. In addition, some highly regulated customers are asking for specialized encryption capabilities for unique workloads.

The new TPU systems we are announcing today address this new reality. Coupled with our recent PyTorch announcements, our aim is to make TPUs more easily accessible to every developer and Cloud customer. By combining modular custom silicon with an open and easy-to-use software stack, we can deliver new hardware and system configurations at the pace of the AI industry. 

Building the computer around the chip

Today, we’re announcing two new TPU systems — and there’s an important difference between a new chip and a new system. 

Designing a new chip means laying out billions of microscopic transistors on a silicon wafer in a multi-year process bound by the laws of physics and a complex, long-duration manufacturing lifecycle. A system, on the other hand, is about how we bring together the compute, networking, and storage around the chip. This can include how they are packaged with the chips, to quickly meet emerging customer needs and research use cases. 

When we built our very first TPU more than a decade ago, we knew AI software would evolve much faster than silicon manufacturing ever could. So we made a foundational bet on system balance and modularity, architecting our TPUs as building blocks as part of our AI Hypercomputer, so engineers could rapidly adjust packaging, high-speed memory, optical networking, and security around them. That approach allows us to deliver specialized supercomputers in a matter of months rather than years.

Specializing for secure, high-context AI

Each system in our eighth-generation TPU portfolio targets a distinct part of the AI lifecycle. TPU 8t and TPU 8i established the baseline for this generation of chips:

  • TPU 8t was designed to be a training powerhouse for massive foundation models with maximum “goodput” — or the useful intelligence delivered per watt of energy used. 

  • TPU 8i is the reasoning engine, designed to break the memory wall, cutting inter-chip communication delays by up to half. 

Now, as enterprises bring autonomous agents into production, we have created two new configurations of these foundational systems to solve two urgent new challenges: hardware-level data security and million-token context scale.

TPU 8tx

TPU 8tx, our third eighth-generation system, is optimized for secure and confidential inference and is also great for small-scale training. It’s built for regulated enterprises and governments running frontier or proprietary models and autonomous agents alongside their most sensitive data. 

Normally, data is encrypted when stored or sent over a network, but has to be unlocked in memory while a computer processes it. Built on the same silicon as TPU 8t and paired with 5th Generation AMD EPYC CPU hosts, TPU 8tx builds security directly into the hardware layer, keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use. And by adopting the same low-latency Boardfly network we created for real-time reasoning, TPU 8tx keeps multi-step agents moving, delivering up to 2x lower latency compared to TPU 8t with a near-zero performance penalty.

Pairing training-grade compute with a fast inference network also means organizations can simultaneously run and customize their models on a single system. TPU 8tx enables teams to fine-tune models using their private data, distill large models into smaller ones, and train their agents through reinforcement learning, all without needing to migrate sensitive data between separate clusters.

TPU 8i Max

Our fourth system, TPU 8i Max, is built for a different problem: the memory wall.

When dozens of AI agents work together across an entire software codebase or hours of video at once, memory bandwidth quickly becomes the bottleneck. So we took two low-latency TPU 8i chips and combined them onto a single package. 

TPU 8i Max scales compute and memory in lockstep, delivering double the compute, double the SRAM and double the HBM bandwidth of TPU 8i, so processors remain equipped with essential data and so that large workloads do not stall. Further, because TPU 8i Max fits twice the silicon within the existing rack footprint, data centers can deploy significantly more computing power per square foot and per watt.

While flexible across workloads, together the four systems in our eighth-generation TPUs give customers a purpose-built accelerator for every stage of the agentic lifecycle. TPU 8t for scale-up training, TPU 8i for low-latency reasoning, TPU 8tx for confidential computing, and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack.

Opening up TPUs to every developer

When we launched the first TPU more than a decade ago, there were only a handful of companies running workloads that needed the processing power of a TPU. The use cases were specialized, so engineers would use optimized frameworks and hand-tuned code. 

Over the years, as AI has advanced, more and more companies began using accelerators. Now, AI adoption is at a point where TPUs are excellent for a wide range of companies and use cases, and as a result, we’ve been working systematically to remove barriers to adoption so that TPUs  are as easy-to-use as general-purpose hardware. 

This investment comes together today across these key areas:

  • Opening up TPU development to every PyTorch developer; no code rewrites needed: Last month, we open-sourced TorchTPU, so PyTorch code and Hugging Face models now run natively on TPUs, alongside out-of-the-box TPU backends for leading open-source inference engines like vLLM and SGLang. And to make hardware optimization effortless, our new open-source TPU agent suite (now in preview) plugs directly into coding tools like Claude Code, Cursor, and Google Antigravity to automate TPU onboarding in minutes, diagnose bottlenecks, and autotune custom kernels using plain language. For production deployments, our new open-source XLA Serving Engine lets you train models in Python and serve them directly in a low-latency C++ runtime across TPUs, GPUs, and CPUs.

  • Industry-leading production performance on InferenceX and AgentX benchmarks: In production, what really matters is outcomes on real AI workloads rather than theoretical peak chip speeds. On industry-standard InferenceX and AgentX benchmarks, which test realistic agentic coding and long-context work, our native vLLM-TorchTPU software stack on TPUs achieved state-of-the-art price-performance marks. New evaluations demonstrate these advantages extend across a wide range of frontier open models and open-source serving stacks while maintaining high model accuracy. Upcoming software optimizations on this same hardware will drive those results even further.

  • Eliminating idle compute waste for autonomous agents: Because AI agents are stateful, they frequently pause for seconds or hours while waiting on a database lookup, an external software tool, or human feedback. To make our agents more resource-efficient during those pauses, our new Agent Compute Engine software automatically suspends and resumes idle sessions, cutting operational infrastructure costs.

  • Breaking through the memory wall with the model-state layer (TPU Sync): Building the computer around the chip also means unifying memory, storage, and networking in software. As agents reason across million-token contexts and continuous reinforcement learning (RL) loops, memory quickly becomes the bottleneck. We’re open-sourcing TPU Sync, the model-state layer for TPU clusters. TPU Sync turns chip HBM, host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network into a single, co-designed memory hierarchy — automatically tiering massive KV caches off the chip in milliseconds, streaming context across disaggregated prefill and decode nodes, and synchronizing RL weights to cut KV transfer latency and Time to First Token (TTFT) by more than 90%.

  • Scaling distributed workloads across TPUs from a single controller: Now generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Cloud Pathways brings the Google DeepMind runtime behind Gemini to every Google Cloud customer. Using a single-controller architecture and pathwaysutils, you can orchestrate large-scale TPU systems across multiple slices as if they were one local machine for pre-training, reinforcement learning, and multihost inference. Cloud Pathways keeps long-running jobs moving through hardware disruptions with colocated Python sidecars, sub-minute slice hot-swapping, and elastic resharding.

  • Stitching custom TPU topologies on-demand with GKE dynamic slicing: Now generally available, GKE dynamic slicing decouples physical hardware provisioning from logical slice formation using optical circuit switching (OCS) technology. By dynamically assembling TPU cubes into larger topologies (super-slicing) or partitioning them into smaller, isolated workloads (sub-slicing) on-the-fly, this update completely eliminates rigid, manual nodepool recreation cycles. This topology agility slashes job startup times by up to 5x and accelerates fault recovery by up to 4.5x, maximizing overall fleet utilization and workload goodput across all TPUs.

Co-designing with a decade of experience

Shipping four TPU systems and a unified, open software stack in a single year only happens when silicon architects, networking engineers, compiler teams, and Google DeepMind researchers build side-by-side. 

Increasingly, we’re even tapping into AI to ideate and build the next generation of AI infrastructure. From using Google DeepMind’s AlphaChip reinforcement learning system to using Gemini to deliver chip layouts in hours rather than weeks, we’re using TPU-powered AI services to rapidly accelerate next-generation TPU hardware development. This is true co-design and a unique Google differentiator. 

Learn more about our new TPU systems by tuning into today’s broadcast at 9 a.m. PT.

item.title: Cloud Pathways, a distributed ML runtime for massive accelerator fleets, now GA
item.description:
Today, we are thrilled to announce the general availability (GA) of Cloud Pathways (Pathways on Cloud) on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) as a core runtime pillar of the Google Cloud AI Hypercomputer.

Originally engineered by Google DeepMind to train and serve Google's frontier models — including Gemini — Pathways is our distributed machine-learning runtime designed for massive, heterogeneous accelerator fleets. In fact, over the last 90 days alone, leading AI companies and global enterprises have processed more than 130 million Cloud TPU chip-hours using Pathways on GKE, across a broad range of TPU generations.

With Cloud Pathways, every Google Cloud customer can use the same single-controller runtime, colocated Python sidecars, and elastic fault tolerance that power Google's largest AI workloads. We are also pleased to announce a Preview integration with Cluster Director to extend Cloud Pathways to Slurm clusters, supporting unified multi-slice JAX execution, elastic training, and interactive notebooks.

What is Cloud Pathways?

As AI workloads scale across thousands of accelerators, spanning multi-slice pre-training, disaggregated inference, and multi-program reinforcement learning (RL) loops, traditional multi-controller setups become harder to program and manage. In default multi-controller JAX, every TPU host runs its own separate Python interpreter with only a localized view of its connected devices and executes the same SPMD program in lockstep, making heterogeneous MPMD workflows and cross-slice resource management complex and brittle.

Cloud Pathways replaces multi-controller management with a unified single-controller architecture built on the open-source Interim Framework Runtime (IFRT). By setting JAX_PLATFORMS=proxy with pathwaysutils, a single JAX client process views and orchestrates multiple large TPU slices, spanning thousands of TPU chips as if they were all connected locally.

Learn more about Pathways in our latest deep-dive blog here.

Core architectural innovations

Cloud Pathways has the following features:

  • Single-controller orchestration: In Cloud Pathways, a single controller manages graph evaluation, persistent Cloud Storage compilation caching, and asynchronous XLA HLO dispatch across TPU slices.

  • Colocated Python sidecars: Client-side colocated Python sidecar containers (with shared-memory support) let you run compute-intensive Python logic such as distributed data loading and checkpointing directly on TPU hosts.

  • Resilient and elastic training: Cloud Pathways decouples job survival from individual slice interruptions with elastic training (pathwaysutils) using host-memory snapshots to dynamically reshard training down to N-1 slices during hardware failures without crashing the client.

  • Interactive mode and Shared Pathways Service: Run, inspect, and debug JAX workloads interactively from a notebook or terminal using interactive mode, or share a long-running pool of Cloud TPU slices on demand across multiple users and jobs with the Shared Pathways Service.

Proven enterprise impact and customer momentum

Frontier AI labs, quantitative research firms, and global consumer platforms have adopted Cloud Pathways to run mission-critical production workloads on GKE, including:

  • Hyperscale multi-host inference: One of the world's largest consumer technology companies runs production batch and reinforcement learning (RL) inference on Cloud Pathways across tens of thousands of TPU v5p, Trillium (v6e), and Ironwood (TPU7x) chips, consuming over 100 million chip-hours per quarter, and co-designed elasticity primitives with Google to expand into pre-training.

  • Elastic pre-training and multi-host RL for scientific foundation models: Google Cloud customer ZenteiQ uses Cloud Pathways on GKE with Cluster Toolkit (gcluster), colocated Python sidecars, and host snapshotting to scale elastic pre-training (MaxText) and single-controller reinforcement learning (MaxText + Tunix) across multi-slice Trillium (v6e) clusters for its scientific foundation models.

"Running multi-day pre-training and post-training jobs on high-cost accelerators requires reliable continuity through both unexpected hardware faults and planned maintenance windows. By running Cloud TPUs and MaxText with Cloud Pathways on the Google Cloud AI Hypercomputer stack, ZenteiQ relies on a proven controller that monitors our TPU topology and dynamically re-meshes and resizes the workload whenever a chip or slice goes offline. Combining Pathways with host snapshotting in production pushes recovery time down to a minimum when disruptions occur, keeping our available TPU capacity fully utilized with very little stall time. Our ML engineers no longer have to spend their hours watching job health or managing manual restarts, and can stay focused on their research workloads." - Prof. Sashikumaar Ganesan, Founder, ZenteiQ

Getting started with Cloud Pathways

Cloud Pathways is generally available today in all Google Cloud regions supporting Cloud TPU v5e, TPU v5p, Trillium (TPU v6e), and Ironwood (TPU 7x) on GKE, with versioned container images (us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways) supporting JAX 0.10.1+. Cloud Pathways is also available in Preview on Slurm TPU clusters in Cluster Director.

To start building with Cloud Pathways:

  1. Read the overview: Explore the Introduction to Pathways on Cloud in the AI Hypercomputer documentation.

  2. Deploy your cluster: 

    1. GKE: Follow the step-by-step guide to Create a GKE cluster with Pathways using Cluster Toolkit (gcluster) or the gcloud CLI.

    2. Slurm: Deploy Pathways via Cluster Director using the step-by-step guide.

  3. Run your workloads: Dive into our production guides for Batch workloads, Interactive notebook mode, Resilient & elastic training, Multihost inference, Porting JAX workloads, and Troubleshooting.

item.title: Powering open infrastructure for autonomous agents
item.description:
As AI shifts from human scale to agent scale, from systems of record to systems of action, and from simple requests to complex agentic workflows, the workload underneath your platform changes completely. An agent works in a continuous, stateful loop: It proposes an action, spins up subagents, executes code or tool calls inside a sandbox, and feeds the results back into the model for the next turn. Running that loop at scale requires the same open foundation and neutral governance that Kubernetes and the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) brought to containers in the 2010s.

Today, we are announcing the donation of Agent Substrate, gVisor, and OpenRL, three open source projects that started at Google, to the CNCF following their acceptance last month into the CNCF Sandbox. To bring this open stack into managed production and accelerate it across TPUs and GPUs, we are also announcing that Agent Substrate has reached its 1.0 milestone and is now generally available as Agent Substrate on GKE.

Each project is now working through CNCF Sandbox onboarding with community maintainers and independent build infrastructure, and gVisor is on a path toward Incubation. These releases deliver an open stack that runs on any Kubernetes cluster, on any cloud, across CPUs, GPUs, or TPUs, by:

  • Scaling isolated agent environments without idle compute overhead with Agent Substrate (now 1.0 and GA on GKE): Agents execute code or tests for a few seconds, then wait on model turns, external APIs, or human input. Keeping a dedicated container alive during those pauses ties up memory and compute. Agent Substrate decouples stateful agent sessions and identities from active compute, snapshotting idle agents to storage and restoring them in under 500 milliseconds to run millions of sandboxes at 10x container density.

  • Isolating untrusted code within a sandbox with gVisor: Agents routinely generate and run unreviewed code and external packages, making standard containers that share a host Linux kernel a security risk. gVisor isolates generated code inside a lightweight userspace application kernel at container packing density on any Linux node.

  • Distributing post training and serving efficiently with OpenRL: Training agents with reinforcement learning (RL) gives builders an open loop to learn across millions of parallel sandboxed rollouts. OpenRL orchestrates self-hosted RL post-training loops in plain Python on Kubernetes.

Scale fully isolated agent environments with Substrate

Agents need isolated compute resources and strict access boundaries, yet spend most of their time waiting: executing code for a few seconds, then pausing while a model reasons or a human responds. They need a discrete identity and central enforcement point to ensure the agent only accesses authorized tools and services without holding sensitive keys. In standard Kubernetes, giving every active agent its own Pod locks up memory and CPU while the agent sits idle, forces the control plane to track millions of persistent objects it was never designed to hold, and ties identities directly to Pods. At the same time, identities are intrinsically tied to Kubernetes Pods, adding exponential complexity for controlling access and secrets.

Agent Substrate solves this by separating the stateful agent from the underlying compute:

  • Actors hold each agent's memory, files, and discrete identity.

  • Workers are reusable execution sandboxes drawn from a warm Kubernetes pool.

  • Gateways enforce inbound and outbound access control and inject secrets based on Actor identity, keeping sensitive keys out of the agent environment.

When an agent pauses to wait on a model turn or tool call, Agent Substrate snapshots the agent’s memory and files to storage and immediately returns the Worker to the warm pool. When the next request arrives, Agent Substrate restores the Actor onto any available Worker in under 500 milliseconds and picks up right where it left off. Think of it as a hotel room rather than a house: you don't keep a room when you leave town, and a new room is ready when you come back.

Since public development started in May 2026, the Agent Substrate project has grown to more than 100 contributors. Early design partners like Nous Research are building Hermes Enterprise on it, and it already powers other CNCF projects like kagent.

Further, reaching the 1.0 milestone shows that Agent Substrate can accept production workloads across millions of sandboxes, achieving 10x the density of standard container runtimes, and performing more than 500 suspend and resume activations per second.

Underneath, you can choose Cloud Hypervisor microVMs or gVisor as your isolation boundary without changing how you manage agent lifecycles. Because Agent Substrate runs standard OCI containers, it works out of the box with Agent Development Kit (ADK) agents, stateful coding environments, and productivity agents.

With today's general availability of Agent Substrate on GKE, you can run this runtime as a managed capability on Google Cloud or deploy the open-source code on any Kubernetes cluster. For teams that want a dedicated microVM compute service through an API without having to manage clusters, Agent Substrate complements Agent Compute Engine, our Titanium microVM service that features fast hibernation and parallel environment-forking for evaluation and RL pipelines.

SPIRITT is building their SPIRITT Workspace, a platform where agents run real work autonomously while humans collaborate to steer the vision, on top of Agent Substrate on GKE. 

”At SPIRITT, every customer gets an autonomous AI workspace where an agent, or a whole swarm of agents, builds, runs, and ships real work across the organization, from code and development cycles to marketing and operations. Agent Substrate on GKE gives us the security isolation to let agents execute code safely, the extensibility to plug in our own runtime, and the density to run every customer's agents economically at scale." - Tamir Magen, CEO, SPIRITT

Isolate untrusted agent code with gVisor

When agents shift from systems of record to systems of action, they run generated shell commands and unreviewed packages. Standard containers share the host Linux kernel with every other workload on the node, which is a risky bet for untrusted code. Hardware microVMs offer a strong boundary, and Agent Substrate supports them natively. Many teams also need strong isolation that runs at container density across any standard Linux instance, even when bare metal or nested virtualization isn't available.

gVisor provides that isolation through a lightweight application kernel written in Go. Sitting between the container and the host OS, gVisor intercepts and handles application system calls in userspace so untrusted code never talks directly to the host kernel. Open sourced by Google in 2018, gVisor runs millions of sandboxes every day underneath GKE Sandbox and Cloud Run. Outside Google, Anthropic and OpenAI use it to contain code execution, Modal and Snowflake run their execution sandboxes on it, and Ant Group and Tencent run it in production at scale.

Three capabilities make gVisor a natural fit for agent fleets:

  • Container density and flexible memory: Unlike VMs that preallocate fixed blocks of RAM, gVisor keeps a container process model where memory scales up and down with the workload, packing more agents onto every node and lowering your cost per agent.

  • Native GPU, TPU, and snapshot support: gVisor supports GPUs, TPUs, and checkpoint/restore natively, so agents can access accelerators inside the sandbox and pause when idle.

  • Runs anywhere Linux runs: Because it doesn't require nested virtualization, gVisor deploys identically across any cloud or local Linux node. Northflank, for example, uses gVisor to sandbox GPU workloads when nested virtualization isn't available.

Donating gVisor to the CNCF clears a longstanding performance barrier for the community. Sandboxed infrastructure providers, including Google, all carry host kernel patches that bring gVisor's I/O performance close to that of native Linux, but upstream Linux maintainers declined to merge them while the project was owned by a single vendor. Moving to neutral CNCF governance opens the path to upstreaming those kernel optimizations, so every builder gets near native performance out of the box. With this move, Ant Group, Modal, and Tines have committed to join gVisor's maintainers, with OpenAI, Tencent, and NVIDIA continuing their contributions.

Scale RL post training on Kubernetes with OpenRL

The sandbox that runs your agent in production is the exact same environment you need to train an agent with reinforcement learning. Today, most frontier capability gains come from RL post-training: running millions of multiturn rollouts inside real tools, scoring the outcomes, and updating model weights. Building that loop yourself usually means forking a monolithic RL framework and debugging distributed weight transfers before you ever touch your training algorithm.

OpenRL brings a clean, self-hosted Python post-training loop directly to your Kubernetes cluster, with:

  • Simple Python primitives: Write your training loop using four clean primitives (sample, forward_backward, optim_step, and save_state) through a Tinker compatible API while keeping your weights and data on your own cluster. Existing tinker-cookbook recipes run unchanged, supporting both LoRA adapters and full parameter fine-tuning.

  • Pluggable engines and Kubernetes scheduling: OpenRL uses Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) to partition your accelerator pool and orchestrate RL work on the shared pool. Its pluggable architecture uses standard engines, including PyTorch/AutoModel for training and vLLM for sampling, with Gemma and Qwen validated out of the box, and with TPU support on the roadmap.

OpenRL also pairs with llm-d, the CNCF distributed inference and RL project founded by Red Hat, Google Cloud, IBM Research, CoreWeave, and NVIDIA that recently reached 1.0, to keep your accelerators busy across both phases of RL. Here, llm-d provides:

  • Prefix-aware rollout routing: The llm-d router routes multiturn rollouts to samplers that already hold matching KV cache prefixes, cutting redundant prefill compute.

  • GPU time-slicing between training and sampling: In RL training, samplers and trainers take turns, leaving one set of chips idle while the other works. OpenRL uses llm-d time-slicing to share the same physical GPUs between sampling and training, reclaiming idle accelerator cycles the same way Agent Substrate reclaims idle CPU and RAM.

OpenRL is the newest layer of this stack by a wide margin. It started in February as a research preview, and we are bringing it to the CNCF early on purpose. Its north star is one recipe for any model on any accelerator, and no single company can get there alone. To get there, you need the people building accelerators (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and TPUs), inference engines (llm-d, vLLM, SGLang), training frameworks, and open-weight models starting with Gemma and Qwen. Setting up neutral CNCF governance before the design hardens makes room for everyone to build it together.

Why the CNCF, and why now

Improving the security and efficiency of AI agents takes joint design across the runtime, scheduler, compiler, and silicon. The past year made the need for affordable, isolated sandboxing and open post-training infrastructure exceedingly clear. Donating Agent Substrate, gVisor, and OpenRL to the CNCF reaffirms Google’s commitment to open collaboration and co-investment. Vendor-neutral ownership lets cloud providers, hardware vendors, and independent software companies participate in the future growth of agentic workloads equally. 

We believe that these donations will accelerate the development and adoption of agentic workloads through these projects similarly to what we saw with Kubernetes.

Come find us at KubeCon

Join us at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City (November 9 to 12) across our sessions and at the Google Cloud booth to learn more about Agent Substrate, OpenRL, and gVisor. You will also hear soon from community partners including Modal, Anyscale, and Tecton on what this open stack means for their agentic workloads. In the meantime, here is where to start:

  • Follow the CNCF Sandbox applications: gVisor #521, Agent Substrate #523, and OpenRL #518, alongside cohort peer KubeRay #525

  • Kick the tires: ate.dev, gvisor.dev, and openrl.dev 

  • Run agents on GKE today: Agent Substrate on GKE, and GKE Sandbox

  • Read the deep dives: Agent Substrate on GKE, gVisor's move to the CNCF, and Introducing OpenRL
