item.title: Introducing Agent Compute Engine and expanded agent governance
item.description:
Blog authors: Nirav Mehta, VP Product Management; Michael Bachman, VP/GM; Kevin Hutchins, VP Product Management

Scaling Gemini to planet scale taught us firsthand that securely running autonomous agents is fundamentally an infrastructure challenge. The shift from single-turn prompting to interactive agents requires a new paradigm of execution and control. To support massive concurrent agent sessions, we engineered new compute and governance solutions for Gemini to help solve these challenges.

Today at AGNTCon + MCPCon, we are delivering these capabilities to customers by launching Agent Compute Engine, a purpose-built compute service that already powers Gemini as an agent for work tasks. It will be available in preview in the coming months, providing hardware-isolated runtime sandbox security. Additionally, we are extending Gemini for business’ agent governance capabilities to support agents wherever they operate. Together, these capabilities deliver the control you need to run, govern, and scale your agents.

Under the hood of Agent Compute Engine

Agent Compute Engine arose from the need to handle Google’s massive agentic workloads that write and execute code, run tools, drive browsers, orchestrate enterprise workflows, and iterate rapidly and at scale. While traditional compute primitives are excellent for standard workloads, they weren't optimized for the unique, highly iterative nature of AI agents.

Purpose-built for agents, Agent Compute Engine gives every Gemini agent its own high-performance, secure computer to act upon, powering Gemini's dynamic, high-churn sessions. Agent Compute Engine is optimized specifically for the unique lifecycle patterns of AI agents, and you will soon be able to use this service to power your own custom agents. Highlights include:

  • Speed with efficiency: Agents start, pause, and resume constantly and require an architecture that delivers speed, at scale, all with extreme efficiency. Agent Compute Engine delivers microVMs that boot rapidly, so an agent loop or an eval sweep doesn’t wait on infrastructure. Further, supporting Google users with multiple agents requires a cost-effective solution that can get the most out of a physical machine. Agent Compute Engine achieves this by using copy-on-write memory sharing to run multiple agents on a single operating system template, and pausing idle microVMs via fast checkpoint and restore. When an agent finishes executing a tool call and enters the “thinking” phase of the agentic loop, the microVM signals that it's idle, and the host moves it from an active to an idle state. In other words, it can pause a running microVM while an agent waits on a human or an external system, and quickly resume it from snapshots.
  • Enhanced security, isolation and governance: As agents take on more complex tasks, the risk of untrusted or adversarial code executing inside a sandbox is an ever-present reality. By running Agent Compute Engine with Titanium, Google’s offload infrastructure processing unit (IPU), we deliver silicon-rooted defense-in-depth built for untrusted AI agents. Agent Compute Engine delivers strong isolation via a hardware-isolated Cloud Hypervisor boundary with its own guest kernel and root access. (For a closer look at Agent Compute Engine’s microVM architecture and security, read the technical deep dive.) Each microVM runs its agent’s own identity, using short-lived credentials. Every microVM also gets its own cryptographically verified ID, and service credentials are injected in egress outside the microVM. Integrated with Agent Gateway, Agent Compute Engine delivers comprehensive observability, policy and security evaluation.
  • Persistence and enterprise integration: Agents require the ability to persist agent data across multiple, long-running sessions. To solve this, each Agent Compute Engine microVM has its own Hyperdisk, enabling persistence of execution workspaces and agent context. In addition, in order to do meaningful work, they need the ability to use enterprise data without moving it. By weaving Agent Compute Engine directly into Google’s cloud and identity fabric, enterprise connectivity is governed by the exact same security and identity model that protects the microVM itself, enabling a unified identity model as well as auditability.

"Scaling the Gemini agent to planet scale requires compute that spins up rapidly and operates with extreme efficiency. Agent Compute Engine microVMs give us the responsiveness, hardware isolation, and workload density needed to deliver interactive agent sandboxes to our users around the world." - Gautham Thambidorai, VP & Google Fellow, Gemini

Building on GKE with Agent Substrate

For platform teams looking for customization and multi-cloud portability, or who have already standardized on Kubernetes, Agent Substrate on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) is an open-source execution runtime that brings the same agent-first design to Kubernetes. It’s built on a zero-trust architecture that cleanly decouples agent execution from machine management. When an agent becomes idle, Agent Substrate snapshots its active memory and returns the machine to the pool, then resumes the agent the moment it’s needed again. Because it’s open source and Kubernetes-native, you can customize it, extend it, and run it alongside your existing workloads. Some Agent Substrate highlights include:

  • High-density: Agent Substrate delivers as much as 10x higher compute density compared to traditional compute while maintaining full kernel isolation and identity-based network security for every agent.
  • Sub-second activation: In benchmark validation running 200,000 agents, Agent Substrate sustained 500 activations per second at less than 500 ms suspend and resume latency.
  • Security by default: Think of Agent Substrate as zero-trust for agents. Each sandbox has strong hardware isolation built in using your choice of microVM or gVisor and every agent gets its own cryptographically secure identity paired with egress proxies that enforce granular network policies and inject credentials outside the reach of the agents themselves. Looking ahead, we will expand the Agent Substrate runtime architecture to integrate with our broader Gemini for business governance framework.
  • Open source portability: Runs on any Kubernetes cluster in any compute environment and works with any agent framework or harness, including Claude Code, OpenClaw, and Hermes.
  • Dynamic storage: Integrates with Filestore agent volumes with sub-second resume latency to scale alongside active compute, providing a single shared workspace for multi-agent workflows.

Leading AI teams like Nous Research are already using this reliable architecture to deploy multi-tenant agents directly into existing customer infrastructure efficiently.

“We built Hermes Enterprise to enable customers to deploy into their existing infrastructure, while handling per-agent isolation and extensible access control. Agent Substrate addresses both at the platform layer in a way that also preserves valuable compute resources. Our experience with Agent Substrate gives us confidence the architecture can scale efficiently as agent workloads grow.” - Hervé Bizira, Chief Business Officer, Nous Research

Expanding governance capabilities for agents everywhere

As organizations transition autonomous agents from isolated pilots to multi-runtime production fleets, traditional security frameworks must be hardened and evolve. Customers face a triple challenge: securing dynamic non-deterministic interaction paths across agents, tools, models, skills and data; maintaining a default deny posture with least-privilege-access distributed runtimes; and ensuring that asynchronous agent actions can be audited. Without strong agent governance, agent sprawl quickly introduces risk — including shadow AI, data exfiltration, and agent actions that are hard to track and audit.

To solve these challenges, we built robust agent governance capabilities into Gemini platform, including:

  • Agent Gateway: Serves as the air traffic controller for client-to-agent and agents-to-anywhere traffic. It integrates a broad set of governance and security policies including sensitive data protection, agent attack protection, semantic governance, and the ability to bring your own policy.
  • Agent Registry: Provides a central repository that serves as the source of truth for all approved running agents, tools, MCP servers, skills, models and endpoints, governing runtime access via applied policies.
  • Agent Identity: Assigns a unique secure ID using open standard based SPIFFE to each agent, acting as the digital signature for authentication, access control, and auditing.
  • Agent observability: Provides OpenTelemetry (OTel)-compliant telemetry adopting agentic semantic conventions, emitting standardized metrics, logs, and distributed traces for every model call, tool invocation, and agent hop across Agent Gateway.

Now as agent fleets continue to grow dramatically across diverse environments, we are extending the reach of our Gemini for business agent governance capabilities across Google Cloud runtimes, cross-cloud, on-prem and client devices to manage and secure agents everywhere they run. This includes the following capabilities:

  • Broad Google Cloud runtime coverage: Extends comprehensive agent governance across Agent Runtime, Cloud Run, Agent Sandboxes in Gemini platform, GKE, and Agent Compute Engine (preview).
  • Consistent cross-cloud reach: Deploys lightweight, Envoy proxy-based policy enforcement points to extend governance to multicloud and hybrid environments (in preview soon).
  • Governance for local agents on endpoints: Extends governance to coding agents like Claude Code and Antigravity CLI on managed devices with an OS-level sandbox and local governance services (in preview soon).

Additionally we are announcing new agent governance capabilities to Agent Gateway to enable granular cost controls, intelligent model routing, and simplified customizations and integrations. Highlights coming this quarter in preview include:

  • Granular token and cost governance: Token management provides control over token consumption across agents and models, allowing you to attribute spend, enforce budget guardrails, and provide a single source of truth for token metrics.
  • Route requests to the right model: Model routing policies route user and agent requests to the right model, controlling costs and improving performance.
  • Extensible policies: Service Extensions bindings add streamlined support for inline programmability and extensibility. Allows tightly integrating Google services, customers’ bespoke functions, and partner services directly into the datapath.
  • Expanded security partner ecosystem: Provides delegated user authorization with third-party identity providers Ping Identity, SailPoint, and Saviynt; in addition to secure Oauth using Agent Identity auth manager. Our extensive list of integration partners is here.
  • Simplified and secure agent-to-tool connectivity: Express Link for Cloud Run allows agents to declare what they need to reach, and it establishes the secure, authenticated connection between components, including identity token injection.

“At L’Oréal, our ambition is to put agentic AI in the hands of our teams, empowering them to bring new ideas to life and shape the future of beauty. Through our Beauty Tech Agentic Platform, AI agents are becoming part of everyday work. Google Cloud’s agent governance provides us the foundation to scale this ambition with confidence, unifying identity, policy and observability across runtimes such as Cloud Run. Our developers can innovate faster while we maintain clear control over what each agent can access.” - Alexandre Frizzo, AI Lead Engineer, L’Oreal

Build on our resilient agent infrastructure

The agentic era requires an evolution in how we scale infrastructure. By combining the high-performance execution of Agent Compute Engine and Agent Substrate with agent governance capabilities from Gemini for business — now expanded with cross-cloud reach — we are establishing a resilient foundation for protected, high-density AI agents.

item.title: ZenteiQ scales batch inference 4x with GKE Inference Gateway powered by llm-d
item.description:
Today we hear from ZenteiQ, an artificial intelligence startup spun out of the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) and selected under the IndiaAI Mission to build sovereign scientific foundation models from the ground up. To pre-train models that understand physical laws, governing equations, and numerical solvers, ZenteiQ designed and built a large-scale batch synthetic data-generation pipeline that runs across multiple model families and feeds verified datasets into training runs. Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and GKE Inference Gateway gave ZenteiQ the inference-routing layer within its pipeline to scale aggregate inference throughput 4.07x and grow daily output from 1.47 billion to 5.97 billion generated tokens for every 1,000 accelerators. - Fisayo Feyisetan, Product Manager, Google Cloud

Unlike general-purpose language models trained primarily on web text and code, scientific foundation models must understand complex physical systems, mathematical governing equations, and numerical solvers across domains such as thermodynamics, computational fluid dynamics, and electromagnetics. At ZenteiQ, we are building sovereign scientific foundation models from scratch that interpret simulation outputs, evaluate equation formulations, and work through step-by-step mathematical derivations that obey physical laws.

Pre-training models on large datasets of governing equations takes hundreds of billions of reasoning tokens. Alongside curated scientific literature and simulation datasets, we also rely on a batch synthetic data-generation pipeline that we independently designed and implemented to generate, evaluate, and filter candidate derivations and solver validation problems before feeding them into our MaxText pre-training jobs.

Because we operate on a fixed compute allocation, every hour our accelerators spend generating and verifying training data is an hour taken away from pre-training. When data generation falls behind, multi-host accelerator clusters reserved for pre-training sit idle, waiting on datasets.

When data generation slows down pre-training

To maximize data generation speed, our pipeline separates prompt preparation on worker pods from model serving on vLLM across multi-node accelerator pools. Each batch moves through four stages: expanding scientific seed concepts into prompt batches, generating candidate reasoning traces with generator models, scoring responses using evaluator models, and running guardrail checks with a separate model family before packaging verified datasets for pre-training.

We originally ran these model pools on Kubernetes with standard ClusterIP round-robin load balancing across inference endpoints. As we scaled our pipeline to feed our 9B- and 35B-parameter model schedules, two routing bottlenecks began slowing down dataset creation.

  • Uneven engine queues: Our upstream worker pods expand seed concepts into prompts of widely varying complexity and response length. Because standard round-robin load balancing had no visibility into vLLM engine queues, it kept sending new requests to serving pods that were already busy processing long reasoning traces, while neighboring nodes had capacity to spare.
  • Redundant prefix computation: Prompts within a generation batch share roughly 70% to 80% of their instructional context and task specifications. Round-robin routing scattered requests with identical instructions across different serving instances, forcing each pod to recompute the same shared prompt prefix from scratch instead of reusing warm caches in accelerator memory.

Together, uneven queues and redundant prefill work caused our generation throughput to swing by as much as half within a single run, stretching out dataset creation and delaying the start of scheduled pre-training runs. We needed routing that understood live vLLM queue depths and prompt caches, without pulling our researchers off model development to build and maintain a custom inference scheduler.

Building on GKE Inference Gateway powered by llm-d

We already run our data preparation and MaxText pre-training jobs on GKE, which lets our team manage data generation and model training on the same Kubernetes platform. Following a recommendation from Google Cloud to address our routing bottlenecks without changing our underlying scientific methodology or pipeline design, we deployed GKE Inference Gateway, powered by the open-source llm-d distributed inference framework, in front of our vLLM accelerator pools.

In our pipeline, worker pods pull scientific seed documents and domain taxonomies from Cloud Storage and expand them into batches of multi-step prompts. Those batches flow through a single GKE Inference Gateway deployment that manages traffic across all of our model families and serving nodes.

Rather than maintaining isolated routing for each model tier, we route generation requests, evaluation queries, and guardrail checks across their respective model pools through the same gateway. Once candidate responses pass evaluation and guardrail checks, worker pods deduplicate and package the verified datasets for direct consumption by downstream MaxText pre-training jobs on GKE.

From round-robin to load- and cache-aware routing

With GKE Inference Gateway and llm-d, routing decisions use live serving signals from our vLLM instances rather than static round-robin rotation. GKE Inference Gateway continuously monitors real-time queue depth and key-value (KV) cache utilization across our vLLM endpoints. When a serving node is busy decoding a long equation derivation, the gateway routes incoming requests to nodes with open capacity, so heavy prompts no longer pile up behind busy workers while neighboring nodes sit idle.

At the same time, the gateway routes requests with matching scientific instructions to the serving node where that prefix’s KV cache is already warm in accelerator memory. Because 70% to 80% of each prompt is shared instructional context while the generated reasoning trajectories vary from request to request, combining prefix-cache locality with live queue balancing lets our pods skip repeated prefill work without overloading any single replica.

Higher throughput, predictable training runs

Adopting GKE Inference Gateway powered by llm-d transformed the speed and predictability of our data generation pipeline. Across our production clusters, intelligent routing delivered:

  • 4x higher fleet throughput: Aggregate throughput jumped from 16,964 to 69,114 tokens per second per 1,000 accelerators — growing daily output from 1.47 billion to nearly 6 billion generated tokens.
  • 3.5x to 5.5x gains across individual model pools: Real-time queue balancing kept serving nodes evenly loaded throughout each run, preventing the mid-run slowdowns caused by long reasoning derivations.
  • 14-percentage-point higher prefix-cache hit rate: Routing prompts with matching scientific instructions to warm caches avoided redundant prefill work before each request branched into its own derivation.

For our research and infrastructure teams, the most important outcome was schedule predictability. Quadrupling daily output meant verified datasets were ready on time, so our multi-host pre-training runs started on schedule instead of waiting on data generation.

What’s next for physical AI at ZenteiQ

As we scale our scientific foundation models from 9B to 35B parameters and beyond, we plan to use the same GKE Inference Gateway and llm-d routing setup for post-training reinforcement learning (RL) and automated numerical solver evaluation loops. Because each turn in those multi-turn rollouts builds on the context of the turns before it, they depend even more heavily on live queue balancing and warm prefix caches.

To try these capabilities on your own workloads, explore the GKE Inference Gateway documentation and check out the open-source llm-d project. You can also read how the Gemini platform team cut latency by 35% with GKE Inference Gateway.

item.title: Hardware-backed security at global scale: Confidential G4 with NVIDIA Blackwell is GA
item.description:
Bringing autonomous agents into production means processing sensitive data and valuable intellectual property in real time. Protecting proprietary model weights, user prompts, and generated outputs requires security that safeguards data while it is actively being computed.

As part of our efforts to enable your enterprise securely, today we are announcing that Confidential Computing on Google Cloud’s G4 instances enabled by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server edition GPUs is now generally available. This release integrates NVIDIA Confidential Computing directly into Google Cloud's AI Hypercomputer, delivering the dynamic performance needed to scale without compromising privacy.

In addition, support for Confidential Space enabling secure multi-party data sharing is rolling out to general availability in the coming weeks.

Protecting sensitive data and models at low latency

Protecting data in use shouldn't mean sacrificing GPU throughput or operational agility. By combining non-exportable hardware keys, verifiable remote attestation, and transparent memory encryption, Confidential G4 helps organizations maximize their investments in agentic and inference workloads. Enterprises can keep costs low while meeting strict regulatory and compliance requirements.

“As organizations deploy AI across increasingly complex cloud, on-premises, and agentic environments, protecting sensitive data is critical. Enterprises must also ensure that AI systems operate securely and consistently with their policies. Google Cloud Confidential G4 VMs powered by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs provide a powerful foundation for privacy-preserving AI and AI operations. Confidential Core AI builds on Google Cloud to transform enterprise principles, policies, and operating requirements into real-time safeguards that monitor and govern AI agents, models, data, and tools. We get hardware-backed provenance from the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, which we bind into the receipt customers get back with their results. Note: Performance results are based on specific testing conditions and configurations. Individual workload performance may vary based on system setup, hardware choice, and software environment.

Our analysis can help you move fast while protecting sensitive data and meeting compliance requirements — a trade-off that real-world deployments are already validating.

”We benchmarked Google Cloud's Confidential G4 against a standard G4 running identical software on our workloads. We found that for a modest 5.2% increase in end-to-end latency, we get a hardware-level assurance that ensures unauthorized users outside our users' attested environment cannot eavesdrop on their conversations. We'd make that trade every time; our users get the convenience of the cloud with the privacy of on-premises.” - Andy Qin, CEO, Vertebrae

Getting started with Confidential G4s

With Confidential G4, improving enterprise security during model execution and agentic workloads doesn't require sacrificing performance, flexibility, or operational simplicity. By providing verifiable trust and robust hardware isolation with near-zero throughput degradation, organizations can securely deploy high-value models and protect critical data assets at cloud scale.

item.title: Simulate, train, and operate robots with Google Cloud physical AI
item.description:
Before a robot can safely pick up a box in a warehouse or work on a factory floor, it needs to be trained to do so. This requires engineering teams to generate massive amounts of synthetic data, train large vision and movement models, and run those models on local hardware with split-second response times. Testing directly on physical machines risks broken hardware, costly downtime, and safety hazards.

Today, we are sharing how Google Cloud physical AI brings simulation, model training, and real-world deployment together on one platform for robotics developers and engineering teams.

Instead of stitching together separate tools for physics simulation, video labeling, GPU training, and edge computing, teams can run the entire robotics pipeline on Google Cloud:

 

Stage 

Workload

Google offering

Simulate 

NVIDIA Isaac Sim , Mujoco, 

G4

Train

Auto labeling video sequences and training VLA /  WMA 

AI Hypercomputer with A3, A4 & ,A5 machines accelerated by NVIDIA  (Cluster Director, GKE, Training clusters on Gemini platform) and Managed Lustre 

Operate

Streaming multi-camera, sensor data and using google model 

GCS, Pub/Sub, Bigquery, Gemini Live, Gemma 4, GDM ER 2

Each stage connects directly to the next, moving training data from virtual environments into production robots and feeding real-world sensor logs back into future training runs.

1. Simulate: Test robots in virtual environments before touching hardware

To speed up testing new robot behaviors, developers can run thousands of virtual environments in parallel on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) using graphics-optimized G4 VMs powered by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. This setup supports physics and simulation tools including NVIDIA Isaac Sim open-simulation framework, NVIDIA Cosmos open world foundation models, and Google DeepMind's accelerated physics engine, MuJoCo Warp.

In these virtual environments, engineering teams can run large-scale reinforcement learning tests, check that multi-camera views stay consistent across angles, and benchmark Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, which link what a robot sees and hears to how it moves. Teams can more easily simulate their use cases without the downtime, hardware costs, or safety risks of physical trial and error.

2. Train: Auto-label video data and train large robotics models

Training robots typically requires huge amounts of labeled video to learn how the physical world works. Google Cloud pairs the Gemini model family with NVIDIA Cosmos to analyze and label video automatically. Because Gemini processes video, audio, and spatial context across long recordings, the toolchain can automatically create bounding boxes, label objects in a scene, and generate VLA training annotations.

Once the data is labeled, teams can move straight into distributed training on Google Cloud's AI Hypercomputer to build and fine-tune large VLA and World Model Architecture (WMA) networks:

  • Fast data storage: Multi-camera video and movement datasets sit on Google Cloud Managed Lustre, a fully managed parallel file system with sub-millisecond latency and terabytes-per-second speed. This keeps GPUs fed with data and speeds up frequent model checkpointing.

  • Direct GPU control: Teams that want bare-metal GPU performance on A3, A4, and A5 VMs can use Cluster Director (for managed Slurm on GCE or GKE) or GKE (natively or via the Slinky Slurm Operator Add-On). It schedules jobs across Google's Jupiter network fabric to keep bandwidth high during large reinforcement learning runs.

  • Managed Training: Teams that prefer not to build and maintain DIY cluster plumbing can use Vertex AI / Training clusters on Gemini platform, which provide managed Slurm orchestration, automated hardware fault recovery, and ready-made recipes for distributed SFT and RL, or serverless custom training jobs for fine tuning.  

3. Operate: Run models on the floor and learn from real-world data

Running robots in factories and warehouses requires both cloud-scale planning and fast local execution. Google Cloud helps teams deploy world models and their own custom agents across cloud, hybrid, and offline environments:

  • Task planning and voice interaction: Gemini Robotics ER 2 (Embodied Reasoning, now in preview  in Model Garden  and the Gemini API in Google AI Studio) turns spatial and physical understanding into step-by-step task plans and multi-robot orchestration for lower-level robot controls.

  • Alongside it, Gemini Live supports visual intelligence and low-latency voice conversations in over 70 languages, so robots can understand what they see and respond to spoken instructions at the same time.

  • On-premises and offline execution: Google Distributed Cloud (GDC) runs managed compute and containers directly on factory and warehouse floors for low-latency camera processing and fleet management. For robots operating without a network connection, lightweight Gemma 4 open models run on local hardware to handle vision, audio, and tool calls in under 10 milliseconds.

item.title: Announcing llm-d 1.0: Open distributed inference for agents on Google Cloud TPUs and GPUs
item.description:
Today at the PyTorch Conference, we released llm-d 1.0, an open-source, Kubernetes-native stack for distributed LLM inference. Co-founded by Google with Red Hat, IBM and others, we worked with a community of more than 500 contributors over 25 organizations on this Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox project, bringing together two important communities: PyTorch, where vLLM and SGLang serve models, and Kubernetes, where distributed systems run and scale in production.

llm-d 1.0 arrives at a time when agents are changing the nature of inference. A year ago, most inference traffic was chat: one prompt in, one response out. Today, workloads are shifting to multi-step agents and reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts that fan out across tools, share long prefixes, and arrive in bursts. Serving them on a single machine — or behind a generic round-robin load balancer — breaks down fast. Replicas recompute the same prompts, accelerator memory fills up with duplicate state, and one bursty agent loop can stall interactive users.

llm-d solves this for teams serving their own models by turning a cluster of model servers into a coordinated serving pool. During the PyTorch Conference keynote, we showed this in action with 1,000 sandboxed agents on Agent Substrate on GKE hitting a single llm-d endpoint across vLLM, SGLang, and a mixed fleet of Google Cloud TPUs and GPUs. As traffic scaled across the three stages below, cache-aware routing and tiered KV cache kept each agent's steps on the replicas holding its context, while flow control queued bursty agent loops so interactive requests stayed fast.

What 1.0 provides

llm-d already delivered prefix- and load-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism and batch inference across Google Cloud TPUs and GPUs. These capabilities provide:

  • Multi-tenant quality of service. Priority and fairness-aware routing via llm-d flow control, helping latency-sensitive requests and bursty agent workloads share a fleet to meet SLOs without starving one another.
  • A stable foundation. v1 APIs and a hardened request path, validated on multiple clouds and accelerator types.
  • Safer upgrades. Router high availability and zero-downtime updates, alongside DisaggregatedSet, which orchestrates prefill/decode-aware rolling updates without dropping context or disrupting active sessions.
  • Agent-aware serving. Session-aware routing, turn-priority scheduling, and native Responses API state, helping agents reuse context across turns.
  • Expanded TPU integration. Native PyTorch model serving with TorchTPU co-operative time-slicing to raise throughput and utilization across Google Cloud TPU fleets.

The components are designed so that you can compose them into your own bespoke production environment. Keep your engine, model and cluster, and adopt only the serving components and configurations you need.

llm-d under the hood

Across the areas below, Google engineers worked with the llm-d community to connect upstream Kubernetes primitives, PyTorch serving engines, and accelerator-aware scheduling into a composable stack.

One endpoint, many accelerators

An agent fleet is not one workload. Interactive turns need low latency, background loops and reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts need high throughput, and demand swings by the minute. llm-d puts your accelerator pools behind a single endpoint, with one router, one KV cache index, and one flow-control policy in front of the whole fleet. Agents call a single API; the router picks the replica for each step and keeps a session's context on the replicas that already hold it. Adding capacity, mixing accelerator generations, or moving a model to a different pool becomes a platform change, not an agent rewrite. TorchTPU brings Google Cloud TPUs into that fleet, running PyTorch models natively inside upstream vLLM and SGLang without model rewrites. For more, see the llm-d on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) TPU guide.

Routing that remembers context

The llm-d router builds on Gateway API Inference, the Kubernetes project for inference-optimized routing that we launched. On GKE, GKE Inference Gateway runs the llm-d router as a managed service, simplifying installation and management and extending routing across regions. The router tracks the replicas holding each cached prefix and weighs load and predicted latency when it picks one. When accelerator memory fills up, rather than dropping it, llm-d uses vLLM’s OffloadingConnector, Mooncake, or SGLang’s HiCache to move KV cache to host memory and then to SSD or Google Cloud Managed Lustre. This setup helps prevent prefix-eviction storms under heavy, multi-turn, and long-context conversational loads across mixed TPU and GPU fleets.

On an agentic coding workload on Ironwood TPU (TPU 7x), prefix-aware routing plus host memory offload cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by more than 85% and raised total throughput 2.4x versus a plain Kubernetes Service, as of October 2026 (source).

Disaggregation that upgrades safely

Prefill is compute-heavy and decode is memory-bound, so running both on the same replicas makes each wait on the other. llm-d runs prefill, decode, and multimodal encode as separate pools, with wide expert parallelism spreading large mixture-of-experts models across nodes. In 1.0, DisaggregatedSet — built on LeaderWorkerSet, the Kubernetes API for multi-host inference that we started — manages these pools as one unit. Rolling updates move prefill and decode together on matching versions while each phase scales independently. For more, see the disaggregated serving guide.

Async inference that runs alongside real-time inference

For latency-tolerant traffic, llm-d 1.0 introduces llm-d-async-processor, which pulls requests from queues like Google Cloud Pub/Sub or Redis and routes them alongside real-time traffic. Using queue and pool-dispatch gates, the processor checks available capacity and enforces strict priority lanes and quotas so background jobs run in slack capacity without starving interactive users.

Time-slicing to put idle RL capacity to work

During RL training, accelerators often sit idle 40% to 60% of the time during rollout generation or weight updates. llm-d now supports Google Cloud TPU and GPU time-slicing to interleave async inference into those quiet cycles, raising aggregate accelerator duty cycles from a ~40% baseline to >70% (source).

Benchmarks you can trust

Tuning a distributed inference stack across routers, KV cache tiers, and prefill/decode pools takes repeatable measurement under realistic multi-turn load. Prism is llm-d’s open-source analysis dashboard for exploring published benchmarks across llm-d’s well-lit paths, backed by standardized llm-d-benchmark recipes and inference-perf workloads. Inspect the exact configurations behind the numbers, or upload runs from your own cluster to compare throughput, latency, and cost curves side by side.

Running llm-d 1.0 on Google Cloud

llm-d builds on Kubernetes components you may already run: Gateway API, LeaderWorkerSet, Dynamic Resource Allocation, Prometheus, and OpenTelemetry. Running llm-d on Google Cloud brings these pieces together with managed infrastructure:

  • GKE Inference Gateway is the llm-d router operating in Gateway Mode, a managed GKE Gateway that handles the L7 proxy and load balancing and calls the llm-d Endpoint Picker on every request, simplifying installation and management so you don't run the proxy yourself. More importantly, GKE Inference Gateway is how you scale llm-d across clusters and regions with global failover and Model Armor safety checks.
  • Autoscaling on inference signals. KEDA and Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) scale pools based on queue depth, saturation, and predicted latency, while Kueue enforces per-model quota on shared accelerators.
  • Mixed accelerator node pools. Google Cloud TPU and GPU pools run behind the same llm-d endpoint, deployed with verified Helm charts.
  • KV cache offloading across layers. Google Cloud Managed Lustre provides a shared remote tier beneath local TPU and GPU HBM and host CPU RAM so long-context workloads run without exhausting accelerator memory.

In production

This GKE llm-d stack carries production traffic, and it has been tested at fleet scale:

  • Gemini platform (formerly Vertex AI) serves production traffic through GKE Inference Gateway, doubling its prefix cache hit rate from 35% to 70%, cutting TTFT by more than 35% for coding agents and cutting P95 TTFT by more than 50% under bursty chat traffic (source).
  • In a published benchmark across a 17,000-node multi-region GKE deployment serving a mixture-of-experts model in the US and Europe, multi-cluster GKE Inference Gateway and the llm-d router scaled throughput 2.9x across three clusters with a 99.9% success rate and less than 1% routing overhead (source).
  • In a published benchmark on A3 Mega cluster serving a 70B-parameter model, llm-d with multi-connector KV cache offloading to Google Cloud Managed Lustre in addition to Host CPU RAM, delivered an approximately 40% improvement in TTFT and a 30% reduction in end-to-end latency responding to 50k-token prompts compared to CPU RAM offload only, while reducing GPU-hour requirements by nearly 60% (source).

Organizations running llm-d on Google Cloud are putting these same capabilities to work in different ways, for instance prefix-aware routing to raise cache hit rates, open interfaces that fit an existing service mesh, and flow control to hold latency for priority tiers when traffic spikes.

“At Snap, we are integrating llm-d into our production AI infrastructure to facilitate high-performance inference at scale. By employing prefix-cache-aware routing, we have achieved prefix cache hit rates ranging up to 75-80%. We appreciate the open-source nature of llm-d, as it enables seamless integration with our Envoy-based Service Mesh." - Vinay Kola, Senior Manager, Software Engineering, Snap Inc.

"At ZenteiQ, we use GKE Inference Gateway powered by llm-d to accelerate synthetic data generation for our sovereign Scientific Foundation Models. By leveraging load-aware and prefix-cache-aware routing, we have achieved over 4× higher aggregate inference throughput, increasing daily generated token capacity from 1.47 billion to 5.97 billion tokens per 1,000 TPU v6e accelerators. The open-source foundation of llm-d, integrated with GKE, enables us to efficiently serve multiple model families at scale without developing and maintaining a custom inference scheduler.” - Prof. Sashikumaar Ganesan, Founder, Zenteiq.ai 

“Serving frontier models across interactive applications and high-volume APIs means handling steep traffic spikes without letting bursty workloads degrade latency for priority customers. With llm-d's prefix-cache-aware routing, flow control and disaggregated serving support we can enforce strict priority bands across our commercial tiers, automatically holding or shedding lower-priority requests when pools saturate so paid traffic meets our latency SLOs. Mistral is a proud supporter of open-source software, and we will continue to contribute back to llm-d and DisaggregatedSet projects.” - Mathis Felardos, Lucas Fernandes-Martins and Nikhil Thomas, Mistral, Inference Engineers and llm-d contributors

Teams serving their own models have been asking for an open stack they can take apart and adapt to their own infrastructure, with the cache-aware routing, traffic control, and upgrade controls required in production. llm-d 1.0 gives them that and a community to build with.

Get started

  1. Check out the full demo of llm-d with TPUs at the Google Cloud booth during the PyTorch Conference.
  2. Deploy llm-d 1.0 on GKE with the verified Helm charts. See the llm-d on GKE documentation.
  3. Start with prefix-aware routing in front of your existing vLLM deployment, then add flow control, KV cache offload (SGlang, vLLM) and disaggregation.
  4. Compare results on Prism and contribute on GitHub.

item.title: TorchTPU is now open source: Run native PyTorch on TPUs
item.description:
Today at PyTorch Conference 2026, we announced a range of new products and integrations designed to help you run PyTorch effectively on Google Cloud or in your own infrastructure. Notably, TorchTPU, our native PyTorch stack for Google TPUs, is now available as open source on GitHub. With TorchTPU, TPUs join GPUs and CPUs as a native option for PyTorch. You can now train, serve, and deploy models on TPUs using the tools you already rely on, including vLLM, SGLang, llm-d, TorchTitan, Ray, TorchRec, Hugging Face, LiteRT. Ultimately, this provides our customers choice across a broad range of workload-optimized computing options including TPUs, GPUs, and CPUs, with a consistent, open software and operational model across the full portfolio.

Run PyTorch code natively on TPUs

Co-developed with the PyTorch team at Meta, TorchTPU lets you run existing PyTorch workloads on TPUs with minimal code changes, using the familiar APIs. TorchTPU lets you debug your models with eager mode, then transition to production-level performance via torch.compile to optimize TPU utilization and reduce memory overhead. By supporting standard PyTorch APIs, advanced diagnostics, and native distributed primitives out of the box, TorchTPU unlocks high performance and operational efficiency from day one.

"At Meta, advancing the frontier of AI requires immense compute scale and deep hardware diversity. We cannot be constrained by a single hardware architecture. TorchTPU is a massive step forward — allowing us to co-develop hardware flexibly with the core machine learning systems team while supporting major LLM, Ads, and Recommendation systems workloads on key production use cases. It enables us to deploy our PyTorch workloads to Google TPUs, provide direct feedback to the engineering teams, and build the ecosystem flexibility everyone needs."- Jana van Greunen, Director of PyTorch Engineering, Meta

We also partnered with Hugging Face so that popular open-weight models across the Hugging Face Hub run natively on TorchTPU. In Transformers v5, deploying models to TPUs is now as simple as passing device_map="tpu". The Diffusers library runs natively on TPUs with support for eager mode, torch.compile, and tensor parallelism to scale large generative models across multiple accelerators. To maintain consistent reliability, we also built dedicated CI/CD pipelines for continuous nightly testing of the Hugging Face Transformers suite on TPU infrastructure.

“Hugging Face is committed to being an open, neutral platform where AI builders can choose the models, frameworks and hardware that work best for them. Hardware diversity is essential to making open-source AI accessible to everyone. Our collaboration with Google to bring native TorchTPU support to our core libraries, including Transformers, puts that commitment into practice. Together, we’re making it easier for the community to run popular models from the Hub efficiently on Google Cloud TPUs using familiar PyTorch workflows. Giving developers more choice in how and where they build helps the entire open-source ecosystem grow.” - Jeff Boudier, VP Product, Hugging Face

Optimizing inference

As reasoning and agentic models scale, inference cost and latency become the primary bottlenecks in production. We’ve integrated TorchTPU into widely used open-source serving engines and paired them with Kubernetes-native fleet routing across TPUs and GPUs to help you optimize throughput per dollar.

This foundation allows developers to scale workloads across diverse hardware while minimizing the friction of platform-specific tuning. To bring these framework-level enhancements to life in production, we have collaborated with leading open-source communities and industry partners. In the sections below, we explore how these partnerships are driving breakthrough efficiency across high-throughput serving with vLLM, structured agentic execution with SGLang, and large-scale distributed fleet orchestration with llm-d.

vLLM: High-throughput serving and memory efficiency

Developed in partnership with Inferact, the native PyTorch vLLM backend on TorchTPU enables developers to deploy open-weight models directly on TPUs with optimized, production-ready serving features and custom Pallas kernels. This integration supports continuous batching, quantization, and multi-chip parallelism on TPU hardware, while preserving upstream worker models, schedulers, and API servers to improve cost-performance ratios, without requiring changes to existing inference stacks.
 

"Our mission at Inferact has always been to make high-performance inference accessible, reliable, and cost-effective across the entire AI ecosystem. We are thrilled to partner on the launch of TorchTPU and bring first-class support for vLLM to TPUs. By bridging PyTorch’s optimized TPU capabilities directly into vLLM, developers can immediately run production workloads on TPUs with the high throughput, low latency, and memory efficiency they expect from our stack." - Simon Mo, CEO and co-founder, Inferact

SGLang: Accelerating agentic and structured workloads

Developed in partnership with RadixArk, our native PyTorch backend for SGLang accelerates highly structured and agentic workloads on TPUs. SGLang uses RadixAttention to reuse KV cache across requests, allowing repeated prompt prefixes to skip recomputation entirely. SGLang-TorchTPU preserves upstream worker models, schedulers, and API servers, using a disaggregation transfer backend that also acts as the I/O backend for HiCache to optimize latency and throughput for complex multi-step generation.

"At RadixArk, TorchTPU has supercharged our development velocity as we roll out SGLang support across diverse silicon. It’s given us a painless path to native TPU acceleration, passing massive efficiency gains and flexible compute choices directly down to our customers." - Banghua Zhu, CTO and co-founder, RadixArk

llm-d for distributed LLM inference

To run inference engines across large fleets, we are releasing llm-d 1.0 with Red Hat, IBM, and a community of more than 500 contributors and 25 organizations. As a Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox project, llm-d connects two open-source communities: PyTorch, where vLLM and SGLang serve models, and Kubernetes, where distributed systems run and scale in production. The llm-d router sends each request to the replica that already holds its context, using prefix-cache-aware routing. It also splits compute-heavy prefill from memory-heavy decode. llm-d 1.0 makes that ready for production with multi-tenant flow control, router high availability, stable v1 APIs, and session-aware routing for agents. On Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), you can have the choice of running on either GPUs or Google TPUs, with a common llm-d endpoint, and choose the hardware that fits each workload.

"At Zenteiq, we use GKE Inference Gateway powered by llm-d to accelerate synthetic data generation for our sovereign Scientific Foundation Models. By leveraging load-aware and prefix-cache-aware routing, we have achieved over 4× higher aggregate inference throughput, increasing daily generated token capacity from 1.47 billion to 5.97 billion tokens per 1,000 TPU v6e accelerators. The open-source foundation of llm-d, integrated with GKE, enables us to efficiently serve multiple model families at scale without developing and maintaining a custom inference scheduler." - Prof. Sashikumaar Ganesan, Founder, Zenteiq.ai

Training at scale

Scaling PyTorch training across thousands of accelerators requires fault-tolerant, compile-aware distributed frameworks. We have integrated TorchTPU into the PyTorch community’s core training, reinforcement learning (RL), and orchestration frameworks.

TorchTitan: Distributed high performance training at scale

TorchTitan is the PyTorch-native reference implementation for scalable distributed training and features a production-grade integration with TorchTPU. By connecting to PyTorch's torch.compile and TorchTitan’s compile friendly SimpleFSDP, specialized Pallas kernels, and graph-level optimizations, developers can build and train models on TPUs with high efficiency at scale.

TorchTitan provides recipes for pre-training large dense models (such as Llama 3 70B/405B, Qwen 3 8B/32B, and MuseGlimmer 30B), Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) such as Qwen 3 235B, and diffusion transformers (such as FLUX.1 12B), and has been validated running with up to 8000 Ironwood TPUs (TPU v7x). Beyond initial pre-training, TorchTitan serves as the scalable trainer inside post-training pipelines like VeRL for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and RL alignment.To test large-scale efficiency on demanding open architectures, TorchTPU’s training paths via TorchTitan demonstrated up to 52% Model Flops Utilization (MFU) on Qwen 3 8B, showing near-linear scaling and stability across up to 8,192 Ironwood TPUs.

VeRL: Scalable post-training and reinforcement learning in preview

RL is a foundational technique for frontier labs that are advancing model capabilities, as well as for enterprises customizing models for domain-specific tasks. Yet, orchestrating distributed RL workloads remains one of the most complex challenges in modern AI infrastructure. Bridging that gap, VeRL has quickly become one of the most popular RL frameworks, supporting everything from verifiable math and coding rewards, to multi-turn agentic tool use at massive scale. 

To help expand hardware choice for this thriving community, we upstreamed a TPU backend and an end-to-end reference recipe to VeRL. Built on a disaggregated trainer-sampler architecture designed to maximize training efficiency, our GRPO reference recipe on mathematical reasoning datasets demonstrates how developers can deploy VeRL workloads on TPUs while preserving their existing, hardware-agnostic model and algorithm code. 

Ray: Orchestrating heterogenous compute

We’ve also added native TorchTPU support to Ray, enabling you to orchestrate PyTorch data processing, training, RL, and serving across CPUs, GPUs, and TPUs within a single workflow. With a few lines of resource configuration, you can schedule each stage of a heterogeneous AI pipeline onto the accelerator best suited for the job.

“At Ray Summit we talked about the PARK stack, PyTorch, AI models, Ray, and Kubernetes, because that's what teams are building production AI on today. TorchTPU embeds Google TPUs directly in that industry-standard stack. We've also worked closely with the Google team to support TPUs as a first-class accelerator in Ray. Coupled with native PyTorch support, teams can now seamlessly develop, scale, and monitor their workloads on TPUs." - Edward Oakes, Chief Architect, Anyscale

Deployment flexibility and operational efficiency

True portability requires standardizing deployment tools across different hardware profiles, including edge devices and cloud accelerators.

LiteRT joins the PyTorch Ecosystem

Many PyTorch models need to run on phones, laptops, browsers, and embedded devices. Today, LiteRT (formerly TensorFlow Lite), Google's high-performance on-device AI inference, joins the PyTorch ecosystem. 

With LiteRT-Torch, you convert a PyTorch model with a single litert-torch.convert() call. It builds on torch.export() and Core ATen operators, so your model code stays in PyTorch. For LLMs, LiteRT Torch exports Hugging Face Transformer models to run with LiteRT-LM. The converted models run on Android, iOS, macOS, Windows, Linux, web, and IoT devices, with hardware acceleration across CPUs (via XNNPack), GPUs (via open source ML Drift), and NPUs from major chipsets provided through a single API. 

TPU agent suite in early preview

To expand Pytorch adoption on TPUs, we are announcing that the TPU agent suite is in preview on GitHub. Integrating through plug-ins with several coding harness-model combinations, the TPU agent suite helps automate onboarding, diagnostics, user questions, and inference performance tuning for many PyTorch models. 

Get started with PyTorch on Google Cloud

Together, these releases reinforce our commitment to making the Google TPU software ecosystem an open, developer-friendly environment for the PyTorch community. By bringing native TPU support upstream into the PyTorch stack across TorchTPU, Hugging Face, vLLM, SGLang, llm-d, TorchTitan, VeRL, and Ray — and contributing LiteRT to the PyTorch Ecosystem — we are giving you the flexibility to build, adapt, and scale AI on your terms.

Visit the Google Cloud documentation to get started running PyTorch on TPUs today.

item.title: Day 0 support for Reflection’s Beam on Google Cloud: 5x faster perf with llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo
item.description:
Today, Reflection released Beam, its first open-weight model built to give developers, researchers, and enterprises open control and customization for frontier software engineering and long-horizon agentic tasks. Released under a permissive Apache 2.0 license with BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoints available at launch, Beam sets a new standard for inference efficiency in the 500B-parameter class by solving complex reasoning and coding problems with 3x to 4x higher reasoning compute efficiency than comparable open models.

Alongside today’s release, Google Cloud is announcing day 0 support and ready-to-run deployment recipes for serving Beam on Google Cloud AI Hypercomputer and NVIDIA AI Infrastructure.

To help developers get the full benefit of Beam’s token efficiency in production, we worked with Reflection to optimize performance of the underlying serving stack using llm-d (with vLLM) and NVIDIA Dynamo (with SGLang) on Google Cloud:

"By deploying our Beam model on Google Cloud, we achieved up to 5x higher performance and 8x lower latency to optimize serving of agentic workloads." - Joe Spisak, VP of Product & Head of Open Source, Reflection

With today’s day 0 release on Google Cloud, developers get:

  • Compounding model and system efficiency: Combining Beam’s 3x to 4x reasoning compute efficiency with system-level optimizations on A4X Max instances (NVIDIA GB300 NVL72) for up to 5x higher throughput and 8x lower latency,* and G4 VMs (NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000) for up to 2x higher throughput and 8x lower latency.*

  • High-efficiency multi-turn serving: KV-cache-aware routing, prefill/decode disaggregation, speculative decoding and hierarchical KV cache offloading to Host DRAM and Local SSD reduce redundant prompt recomputation across long coding sessions.

  • Turnkey optimized deployment: Our recommended performance optimized recipes for agentic workloads with llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo are available in AI-Hypercomputer/gpu-recipes, llm-d repo and Model Garden in Gemini platform with a few clicks. 

*Based on customer benchmarking

Scaling inference requires system-level optimization

When evaluating models for agentic coding and tool use, inference efficiency happens at two distinct layers: how efficiently the model reasons and how efficiently the serving system executes multi-turn loops.

Model-level efficiency: Reflection’s Beam

Reflection designed Beam (~501B total parameters with ~23B active parameters per token, and an approximately 1M-token context window) specifically for text-native software engineering and multi-step tool use. It plugs directly into the coding harnesses developers already use, including Reflection’s Mirror CLI, Claude Code, Hermes, OpenCode, and , to resolve GitHub issues, run CLI and DevOps workflows, and complete long-horizon tasks.

Because Beam activates only 23B parameters per token and reaches solutions using 3x to 4x fewer reasoning tokens than other comparable open weight models, it dramatically reduces the inference-time compute required for each reasoning step.

System-level efficiency: AI Hypercomputer optimized serving

Once developers deploy an agent into production, a second set of bottlenecks could appear at the serving layer. In an agentic coding loop, the model is called dozens of times in a single session. With every turn, the coding harness appends new file reads, code diffs, compiler logs, and tool outputs to a shared conversation history that quickly grows to tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens.

Even when the model itself generates 3x to 4x fewer reasoning tokens on each turn, the accumulated context window across turns creates two major infrastructure challenges:

First, prefill compute becomes a bottleneck. Standard Kubernetes load balancers distribute requests using stateless round-robin routing. When a coding harness sends Turn 15 of a session, it often lands on a different replica than Turn 14. That replica is forced to recompute the entire historical prompt from scratch, wasting GPU compute and creating long prefill queues that delay other users.

Second, decode becomes bottlenecked by KV cache capacity. Holding long-context KV caches for dozens of concurrent agent sessions quickly fills up GPU High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM). Once HBM fills up, the serving engine has to evict older KV blocks. As soon as those blocks are evicted, cache hit rates drop and GPU throughput stalls.

To preserve Beam’s model-level efficiency at cluster scale, the serving stack has to be optimized as a distributed system. That is why our recipes pair Beam with llm-d (with vLLM) and NVIDIA Dynamo (with SGLang).

Inside the AI Hypercomputer inference architecture

To run Beam’s BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoints at peak efficiency on Day 0, we designed a vertically integrated architecture on AI Hypercomputer where each layer handles a specific part of the agentic serving lifecycle.

Rather than treating inference pods as stateless endpoints, each layer of the stack is co-designed around the multi-turn agent lifecycle:

  • Prefix- and load-aware routing (GKE + llm-d EPP / Dynamo router): Tracks cached prefixes and queue depth across worker pods, steering each follow-up turn from a coding harness to the replica holding its warm KV prefix while preventing queue saturation via turn-priority flow control.

  • Disaggregated compute and speculative decoding (A4X Max & G4 instance): Runs vLLM and SGLang with native Blackwell NVFP4, Expert Parallelism (EP) for Beam’s 23B active experts, Data-Parallel Attention, and DFlash2 speculative decoding. Separating Prefill and Decode (P/D) pools ensures heavy prompt bursts never stall active token generation.

  • Tiered KV cache (GPU Memory -> DRAM & Local SSD) Active KV blocks stay in high-bandwidth GPU memory (Tier 1), while warm KV blocks evicted during long-horizon sessions overflow into host CPU DRAM and local NVMe SSDs (Tier 2) via vLLM’s OffloadingConnector or SGLang's HiCache, allowing historical context to be fetched in milliseconds instead of recomputed from scratch.

System optimizations for multi-turn agentic workloads

When serving multi-turn coding and tool-use workloads like the AgentX trajectory dataset across rising concurrency levels, each layer in the serving stack contributes to the performance and latency improvements for multi-turn, long context traffic patterns of agentic workloads:

A note on reading these charts. The two configurations are not comparable to each other. NVIDIA Dynamo ran on A4X Max instances with 32 x NVIDIA GB300 NVL72GPUs; llm-d ran on G4 VMs with 8 x NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. Each chart shows the gain over a baseline on the same hardware. More replicas give the router more warm KV caches to hit and more room to split prefill from decode, so the uplift grows with the deployment. Both llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo scale up and down to match the underlying infrastructure.

Across both platforms, layering these optimizations shifts the Pareto frontier to deliver higher output throughput and faster per-user interactivity simultaneously:

  • Baseline deployment (Stateless round-robin routing). In a standard Kubernetes deployment without prefix awareness, consecutive turns from the same coding session land on different replicas, forcing constant prefill recomputation on historical context and causing throughput to plateau as concurrency scales.

  • KV-cache-aware & flow control routing. Enabling prefix-aware routing in NVIDIA Dynamo or llm-d’s Sticky EPP with turn-priority flow control keeps multi-turn agent trajectories pinned to the replica holding their warm KV cache, immediately cutting Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) latency and freeing up GPU compute, resulting in a significant increase in token throughput.

  • Host DRAM and Local SSD (LSSD) KV offloading. Offloading evicted KV blocks from GPU memory into host DRAM and local NVMe SSDs prevents cache thrashing when dozens of long-context coding sessions exceed on-device GPU memory capacity.

  • Disaggregated serving, speculative decoding, and KV pool tuning. Tuning hybrid KV cache memory allocation, enabling speculative decoding, and disaggregating prefill and decode workers isolates token generation from heavy prompt bursts while the draft model multiplies output throughput to keep per-agent token interactivity fast.

Get started and meet us at PyTorchCon and GTC Berlin 

This blog explored how you can leverage system level optimizations to scale performance to serve Reflection's Beam family of models for agentic workloads. item.title: Architecting autonomy: A design pattern for high-compute, governed agents in biotech
item.description:
In production systems today, most AI agents operate as lightweight dispatchers. They parse a prompt, make an API call, retrieve a record, and hand back control. Their execution is fast, stateless and cheap. Biotechnology does not work this way. 

Folding a protein target, screening a 50,000 compound ligand library, or evaluating structure-activity relationships (SAR) are not quick API lookups. They are sustained, stateful, GPU-bound simulations that run for minutes or even hours across specialized silicon. When you ask a general-purpose large language model (LLM) endpoint to coordinate a complex drug discovery workflow, the standard paradigm breaks: Timeouts occur, context windows overflow with atomic coordinates, and proprietary chemical Intellectual Property (IP) risks exposure to external networks. 

Building enterprise grade research and development (R&D) agents requires moving past the monolithic assistant model. In this blog post, we will discuss how to use a three-layer architecture: separating cognitive orchestration (the brain) from computational execution (the muscle), and anchoring both inside an enterprise governance plane to build scalable agents for drug discovery use cases in biotech.

A three-layer pattern

The reference architecture below shows how to architect, optimize, and govern high-compute autonomous agents in biotechnology, specifically Drug Discovery.

The execution layer: scaling the muscle - high-compute execution 

The execution layer is responsible for the heavy scientific computations. The first architectural decision is determining where workloads should run:

  • Strategic, proprietary pipelines require dedicated GPU infrastructure within your security perimeter

  • Routine or standardized workloads can safely be delegated to managed cloud endpoints

In this architecture, protein folding is driven by ESMFold and generative design by GenMol. Both run as NVIDIA Inference Microservices or NIMs deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) using G4 VMs backed by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs.

A critical hurdle in containerized GPU workloads is the cold-start penalty, the latency delay required to pull multi-gigabyte model weights from an image registry and stage them into GPU memory (VRAM).

To ensure low latency responsiveness, we build the following as a recommendation into the reference architecture:

  • Maintain warm pools: Pin the GKE node pool to a minimum of one active node.

  • Preload weights: Model weights are loaded directly into VRAM at pod initialization, ensuring containers are immediately ready for inference.

  • Resilient scheduling: GKE manages pod lifecycles and restarts failed instances without tearing down the underlying VM infrastructure. 

This approach trades custom, manual CUDA kernel tuning for NVIDIA's pre-compiled, containerized runtimes, dramatically reducing infrastructure engineering overhead while ensuring deterministic throughput.

In biotech, chemical structures represent millions of dollars in proprietary IP. A docking request transmits SMILE strings or 3D coordinate matrices that must never leave company custody.

Containerized NIMs eliminate the friction between rapid prototyping and rigorous data isolation. During early exploration, researchers can query NVIDIA hosted endpoints. When transitioning to proprietary lead candidates, the exact same container is deployed to GKE inside a private VPC. The agent’s orchestration logic remains identical; only the target URI updates from an external proxy to an internal VPC endpoint. No structural data leaves the enterprise perimeter.

The cognitive layer: Multi-agent reasoning

With compute execution isolated, the cognitive layer manages agentic workflow sequencing. Built on Agent Runtime, within the Gemini platform, this reference architecture shows a system that deploys a hierarchical multi-agent structure, one lead orchestrator, and two specialized domain sub-agents (Lead Optimization and Safety Screening) . The multi-agent design can be modified to suit the use case at hand. 

Based on this design, when an end-user submits a high-level task such as “ Analyze Candidate 4b against Target X and produce a SAR report”, the system applies four core orchestration patterns discussed below; 

  • In-process native agent handoffs: The lead orchestrator delegates tasks to specialist sub-agents using Agent Runtime’s native SDK rather than network-serialized agent-to-agent HTTP protocols. This eliminates intermediate network hops and keeps internal handoffs instantaneous. Only the outermost boundary communicates outward to user-facing surfaces like the Gemini agent.
  • Passing bulky payloads by reference: LLMs degrade quickly when forced to ingest massive arrays of 3D spatial coordinates. In this architecture, raw structural data (PDB files, docking poses, trajectory logs) is written directly to Cloud Storage. Agents pass lightweight, signed object URIs and high-level structural summaries, keeping context windows compact and inference costs down.
  • Decoupling workflow logic from biochemical reasoning: General-purpose LLMs excel at task planning and synthesis, but are prone to hallucinating biochemical nuances. To control this behavior, this architecture maintains strong separation of concerns, namely, workflow and tasks decomposition are handled by Gemini. Domain chemistry and pharmacological reasoning are handled by specialized Nemotron models hosted on dedicated GPU nodes. 
  • Context-driven evaluation over rigid cutoffs: Traditional computational screening enforces arbitrary numerical cutoffs (e.g., discard if binding affinity ,-7.5 kcal/mol) However, therapeutic context fundamentally alters risk tolerance. Preventive cardiovascular therapy taken daily by healthy patients requires extremely strict safety margins, or a novel oncology candidate targeting an intractable cancer may accept higher toxicity if efficacy is demonstrated.

By passing disease context directly into the specialized reasoning models, drug candidates are evaluated against dynamic, target-specific profiles rather than static thresholds, preventing the premature culling of viable drug leads.

Performance best practices for high-compute pipelines

Optimizing an agentic system that interfaces with heavy GPU compute requires challenging common engineering instincts:

Common Assumption

Architectural Reality

Recommended Best Practice

"Swap in a faster driver model to cut latency."

The primary orchestrator's token generation is rarely the bottleneck in multi-step R&D pipelines.

Optimize I/O, not token speed: Focus on reducing payload sizes and intermediate network hops rather than compromising orchestrator reasoning depth.

"Parallelize tool calls across workers."

External scientific services and containerized models often serialize requests internally on dedicated hardware.

Respect execution topology: Align client-side concurrency with backend queue mechanics to prevent pipeline lockouts and connection timeouts.

"Pass full simulation states between tools."

Large JSON bodies cause schema validation failures, prompt truncation, and token bloat.

Pass heavy payloads by reference: Store raw coordinates in object storage and pass lightweight URIs between agent boundaries.

"Return outputs only when the pipeline finishes."

Long multi-minute runs leave scientists blind to whether jobs are proceeding or stalled.

Stream intermediate stage completions: Emit progress updates at each completed milestone (e.g., folding complete, docking running) for real-time visibility.

"Chain multiple granular micro-tools."

Deep tool-chains increase the probability of hallucinated arguments and schema mismatches.

Collapse compute pipelines: Wrap end-to-end simulation pipelines behind a single, clean tool interface that takes clear parameters and returns a consolidated object.

The enterprise governance and asymmetric autonomy

Deploying high-compute agents in enterprise environments requires robust data sovereignty, audit trails, and process control. The Gemini platform establishes these safeguards natively with the following components: 

  • Agent Identity: Every autonomous agent operates with a cryptographically verifiable identity. Thus, for a biotech use case, when a candidate molecule is advanced or rejected, the event is permanently logged to that specific agent principal. 

  • Agent Gateway: This serves the single ingress/egress point for every interaction within the perimeter. Centralized IAM and regional residency rules help ensure sensitive molecular data remains within designated cloud regions. 

  • Agent Registry: This feature maintains a curated catalog of approved agents, validated tool schemas, and authorized Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, preventing rogue tools from executing in production. 

  • Model Armor: This functionality inspects incoming prompts and outgoing payloads in real time to prevent prompt injection and data exfiltration. 

The payoff is clear. Identity, RBAC, auditing, residency, and data protection are native properties of the Gemini platform; this allows enterprise customers to focus on science rather than having to build a compliance stack for every project. 

In high-stakes research and development, full autonomy introduces unacceptable liability, while requiring approval for trivial steps can create frictions. The solution addressing this to use asymmetric gating in the following ways;

Automate reversible operations: For example, allow the agent to resolve chemical naming synonyms, pull structural PDBs, and run preliminary Lipinski screens autonomously without interrupting the researcher.

Gate irreversible operations: For instance, initiating multi-GPU docking run, advancing a lead compound to wet-lab synthesis, or archiving a therapeutic program must require explicit human sign-off.

The pattern, and the path forward

High-compute autonomous agents succeed when the boundaries between cognitive planning, numerical computation, and system governance are clean in the following ways:

  1. Keep the orchestrator focused on decomposition and synthesis, leaving intensive biophysical simulation to specialized, containerized microservices and models.

  2. Eliminate context bloat by passing complex chemical data by reference through cloud storage.

  3. Anchor the workflow in enterprise governance, pairing cryptographic agent identity with asymmetric human oversight.

As generative and structural biology models expand toward whole-cell modeling and complex dynamic simulations, this decoupled architecture ensures research systems scale efficiently while keeping proprietary IP secure and auditable.
